detail.title: Moral Legitimacy and Market Exit Strategies: How Home-Country Consumers Evaluate Firm Responses to Economic Sanctions
detail.abstract: Economic sanctions are increasingly used as tools of international norm enforcement, yet little is known about how home-country consumers evaluate firms' strategic responses to such measures. This research examines how different market exit strategies from sanctioned host countries affect home-country consumers' legitimacy judgments and support for firms. Drawing on legitimacy theory and research in international business, we develop and test a framework to explain how home-country consumers respond to full, partial, and no-exit strategies. Across four studies using longitudinal secondary and experimental methods, we find that home-country consumers react more positively to firms that pursue full exit from a sanctioned market than to those that adopt partial or no exit strategies. Individual-level differences in susceptibility to normative influence, cognitive empathy, individualism, and ethical views on the use of sanctions shape these evaluations. The findings contribute to theories of legitimacy, international divestment, and moral stakeholder evaluation, and offer practical guidance to firms navigating the complexities of operating under economic sanctions.

title: The Effect of Legalized Sports Betting on Convenience Store Lottery Sales

detail.title: The Effect of Legalized Sports Betting on Convenience Store Lottery Sales
detail.abstract: In this study, we investigate the effect of sports betting legalization on convenience store lottery sales. We posit that there are two main relevant effects: (1) a substitution effect, which decreases lottery sales due to people substituting lotteries for sports betting, and (2) a spill-over effect, which increases lottery sales due to sports betting increasing people's taste for or addiction to gambling. Our main hypothesis is that online sports betting (OSB)'s effect on lottery sales is weakly more positive than the effect of retail sports betting (RSB). Our results lend support to this. Particularly, using a store-month panel dataset, we find that the launch of OSB led to a 17.3% increase in monthly lottery sales, and that the launch of RSB led to a 16.4% decrease in monthly lottery sales. This is consistent with the case where the spill-over effect dominates for OSB and the substitution effect dominates for RSB. For states that launched OSB and RSB during the same month, we find no significant effect on lottery sales, implying that the effects of OSB and RSB tend to cancel each other out. These findings could be useful to policymakers in evaluating the costs and benefits of legalizing sports betting, especially from a tax revenue standpoint.

title: Mental Health and the Early Career Dynamics of Young Men
affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis - John M. Olin Business School, Washington University, Saint Louis - John M. Olin School of Business , Washington University in St. Louis - John M. Olin Business School and Washington University in St. Louis - Department of Economics

detail.title: Mental Health and the Early Career Dynamics of Young Men
detail.abstract: Do poor mental and physical health scar early career labor market trajectories? Using longitudinal data from the Household Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA), we document the life-cycle patterns and analyze the two-way interactions between health and labor market outcomes. To address health endogeneity, we exploit exogenous life shocks as instruments, identifying the negative short-run effects on health. Building on this evidence, we develop a dynamic discrete choice model with unobserved heterogeneity, allowing for correlation between health and income. Our estimates show that poor health, especially mental health, significantly reduces the likelihood of full-time employment and raises the probability of not working relative to part-time work. A strong scarring effect of mental health shocks emerges, leading to persistently weaker recovery paths and lower earnings. Our counterfactuals highlight three findings: (i) permanent health and income types jointly drive large inequality, with low types earning half as much as high types; (ii) persistent poor mental health contributes to higher earnings inequality than physical health; and (iii) transitory health and labor market shocks have long-run negative effects on labor supply choices, amplified with poor mental health. By jointly modeling the dynamics of mental and physical health, we disentangle their distinct roles, show how health shocks scar individuals over the life-cycle, and highlight the importance of early mental health interventions for sustaining productivity and reducing inequality.

title: Loyalty and Preference in Sustainable Product Choice
affiliations: University of Hawaii at Manoa - Department of Marketing, Dartmouth College - Tuck School of Business and New York University (NYU) - Center for Sustainable Business

detail.title: Loyalty and Preference in Sustainable Product Choice
detail.abstract: Repeat purchase rates critically affect the expected customer lifetime value (CLV). These rates are determined by customer loyalty to the previously purchased product or brand (state dependence) and baseline consumer preferences for that product. In this paper, we examine both components for consumer packaged goods that utilize onpackage sustainability labels in comparison to those without such labels. Examining data in five consumer packaged goods categories for 64,298 households across the US between 2015 to 2021, we find that consumers are loyal not only to brand but also to the specific sustainability labels. Furthermore, households in our sample tend to have lower mean preferences and lower dispersion of preferences for sustainable products, indicating that sustainable products are seen as closer substitutes with each other than non-sustainable products with other non-sustainable products. With similar product margins, this would imply lower CLV for sustainable products. Our results suggest that, although sustainability labels can increase the loyalty to a set of products, they do not serve as a substitute for brand value in generating higher CLV.

title: The Heterogeneous Effect of Dropping Out for Higher Education Students: The French Case

detail.title: The Heterogeneous Effect of Dropping Out for Higher Education Students: The French Case
detail.abstract: For higher education systems with general and vocational degrees, the question of resource allocation for dropout policies is fundamental. In France, the university concentrates most of the focus and resources compared to the vocational track. I estimate the heterogeneous effect of dropping out on labor market outcomes (employment rate and wages), conditional on the student’s degree, to evaluate the validity of this allocation. I use a causal Random Forest methodology to account for the heterogeneous cohort composition of these degrees, with the distance to the closest higher education institution as an instrument for dropout. Using 2SLS leads to underestimating the overall effect of dropping out by 9 percentage points for the employment rate and by 4 percentage points for the average wage. Vocational degree dropouts are more penalized than university dropouts on their average wage but not on their time in employment. Finally, using a multidimensional categorization of students can be beneficial for creating a targeted dropout policy.

title: Measuring Markups: Revisiting the Cost Accounting Approach

detail.title: Measuring Markups: Revisiting the Cost Accounting Approach
detail.abstract: Among the ways to measure market power, special attention has always been given to the wedge between marginal cost and price: the markup. This paper investigates the validity of firm-level markup estimation techniques, focusing on the cost accounting (CA) approach—a straightforward, transparent, and data-thrifty alternative that, despite its origins in the early industrial organization literature, has seen little modern application. While the production function (PF) approach has quickly become the workhorse method in macroeconomic applications, several high-profile criticisms have brought its validity into question. My findings show that the rise in U.S. markups is robust to CA, suggesting that the trend is not driven by biases. In fact, variation in PF estimates is driven almost entirely by variation in its 'accounting component,' rather than its 'production function component,' which contains the well-known biases. For validation, I develop a novel test based on Dorfman-Steiner's (1954) advertising equation, concluding that the cost accounting approach provides a much higher signal of underlying markups in some cross sections, though both measures offer signal of underlying markups. The data-thrifty nature of CA makes it feasible for a broader range of applications. To highlight this, I conclude with several applications that play into CA's strengths. Collectively, these results suggest that CA should be preferred to PF in some cases, although it can sometimes be useful to try both.

detail.abstract: This study examines customer perceptions and satisfaction with mobile banking services in Maharashtra, India, focusing on how these perceptions vary across different occupational groups. A total of 573 respondents from six districts of Maharashtra (India) participated in an online survey using a 3-point Likert scale. The study investigates several key factors affecting the quality of mobile banking services, including ease of use, scope, speed, privacy, safety, reliability, responsiveness, cost-effectiveness, usefulness, and app appearance. title: Cyber Risk in Banking: Measuring and Predicting Vulnerability

detail.title: Cyber Risk in Banking: Measuring and Predicting Vulnerability
detail.abstract: We construct a bank-quarter panel linking external cybersecurity ratings, realized cyber incidents, and regulatory financial data for U.S. banks (2015-2024). Using quarterly rolling-window random forest models with dynamic feature selection, we predict whether a bank will experience a cyber incident within the next year. Both bank characteristics and cybersecurity posture provide independent and complementary predictive content, with the combined model achieving the highest out-of-sample accuracy. Predictive performance remains robust across bank sizes and forecast horizons and is not driven by simple persistence in incident history. Interpretation of the fitted models highlights the consistent importance of size, balance sheet composition, and specific security controls, along with interactions between these controls, in predicting cyber incidents.

title: The Enduring Legacy of Educational Institutions: Evidence from Hyanggyo in Pre-Modern Korea

detail.title: The Enduring Legacy of Educational Institutions: Evidence from Hyanggyo in Pre-Modern Korea

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: This study examines the long-term impact of Hyanggyo, state-sponsored educational institutions established during the early Joseon Dynasty in Korea (1392-1592), on human capital accumulation. Although these schools largely ceased functioning as educational centers by the late 16th century, their influence has endured to the present day. Drawing on a newly constructed township-level dataset, we find a robust positive association between historical exposure to Hyanggyo and modern educational attainment. This relationship appears to be driven by enduring local demand for education, supported by three complementary findings. First, regions with greater historical exposure experienced larger gains in Japanese literacy during colonial era school expansions. Second, residents in these areas express stronger pro-education attitudes today. Third, historically exposed regions exhibited lower fertility rates, consistent with a quantityquality tradeoff in parental investment. Together, our findings highlight the lasting legacy of early educational institutions.

title: Project Management and New (Social) Media Maturation of a Science and Decline of an Aristocracy
affiliations: University of Birmingham

detail.title: Project Management and New (Social) Media Maturation of a Science and Decline of an Aristocracy
detail.abstract: Project management has matured through crisis. Each great excitation-from war to oil shocks to globalisation-reshaped its tools and meanings. The field once rested on an aristocracy of lauded managers, their prestige secured by mega projects and retold through case study orthodoxy. Alongside them, academic gurus shaped narratives: Robert McNamara importing RAND's scientism into the World Bank, Albert Hirschman offering the romantic optimism of the Hiding Hand, and, later, Bent Flyvbjerg puncturing both with empirical critique of megaprojects. Today, new media unsettles the balance. No longer can aristocrats hide behind glossy reports or scholars preach unchallenged. Failures, biases, and hidden assumptions are exposed in real time. Contestation has entered the open agora. That contestation is science: conjecture, critique, falsification. In shedding aristocracy and postgraduate ritual, project management is entering a phase of mathematization-a rigorous, adaptive science of projects, forged in openness and complexity.

title: Interviewing With Algorithms: The Role of Non-Functional Attributes in Shaping Algorithmic Evaluation Experience
affiliations: University of Georgia - C. Herman and Mary Virginia Terry College of Business, Arizona State University (ASU) - W.P. Carey School of Business, Indiana University Bloomington - Kelley School of Business and National Taiwan Normal University

detail.title: Interviewing With Algorithms: The Role of Non-Functional Attributes in Shaping Algorithmic Evaluation Experience
detail.abstract: Algorithmic evaluation is increasingly used across domains such as credit, education, and hiring, raising concerns that opaque and impersonal systems heighten stress for those being assessed. Job interviews, already stressful, exemplify this trend, where, in judging candidates, algorithmic systems affect the very behaviors they measure. In such high-stakes contexts, this can affect their downstream performance which is typically endogenous to interview behavior. Addressing these concerns, however, requires approaches that can improve candidate experience without altering evaluation, which in such contexts is often constrained and less flexible than in others, such as recommendations or personalization. We identify one such lever: non-functional algorithmic attributes, i.e., features such as the gender, appearance, or voice of an AI interviewer, that do not affect decision outcomes but can influence candidate experience. We theorize and test how offering choice over these attributes improves individuals' reactions and performance in algorithmic evaluation. In Study 1, a field experiment within the hiring process of a leading video-interviewing platform, candidates who could choose their AI interviewer's gender performed significantly better. In Study 2, a controlled online experiment, we replicated this effect and examined its mechanisms. Drawing on procedural justice theory, we distinguished between an instrumental pathway (choice evoking perceived control) and a non-instrumental pathway (choice alleviating fairness concerns). Our findings reveal that the effect arises not from perceived control but from heightened fairness perceptions, which reduced anxiety and enabled stronger performance. Robustness checks ruled out alternative explanations, including concerns for superficial performance gains, gender effects, and social desirability bias. Overall, this research contributes to work on algorithm evaluation, equity, and procedural justice by showing how algorithmic evaluation may introduce flexibility of offering symbolic, outcome-indifferent choices in traditionally rigid processes, thereby enhancing fairness perceptions and candidate outcomes. Such choice is a scalable and legally tractable design lever for reducing anxiety and improving experiences in high-stakes algorithmic evaluation.

title: Why Perspective Matters in Health Technology Assessment: A New Zealand Case Study of HPV Vaccination, Smoking Cessation Programmes, and Hepatitis C Therapy

detail.title: Why Perspective Matters in Health Technology Assessment: A New Zealand Case Study of HPV Vaccination, Smoking Cessation Programmes, and Hepatitis C Therapy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has previously advised both Australian and New Zealand Health Technology Assessment agencies.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This work is based on published simulation models and parameters, and as such did not use data from human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was unfunded.

detail.abstract:
Background
Health technology assessment (HTA) in New Zealand commonly adopts a health-system perspective, which can undervalue interventions with wider societal impacts.

Methods
We built cohort Markov models for HPV vaccination, smoking cessation programs, and hepatitis C antiviral therapy. Lifetime horizons (annual cycles), 3% discounting, and a $50,000/QALY willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold were used. We compared health-system and societal perspectives (productivity, out-of-pocket, and informal care), conducted probabilistic sensitivity analysis (10,000 iterations) and estimated EVPI/EVPPI.

Results
From the health-system perspective, ICERs were cost-saving (dominant) for HPV vaccination, $1.80/QALY for smoking cessation, and $14,657/QALY for hepatitis C therapy. From the societal perspective, HPV vaccination and smoking cessation became more favourable (dominant and cost-saving, respectively), while hepatitis C remained cost-effective with a higher ICER ($26,435/QALY). Productivity effects were the largest societal component. Societal net monetary benefit (NMB) rose by $73m for HPV and $43m for smoking cessation; for hepatitis C it decreased by $12m due to high upfront treatment costs. Decisions were concordant across perspectives at NZ$50,000/QALY.

Conclusions
Incorporating a societal perspective materially increases estimated value for preventive and behavioural interventions in Aotearoa New Zealand. Curative, high-cost therapies may remain cost-effective but show smaller societal gains. HTA processes that transparently include societal costs and benefits could support more balanced and equitable resource allocation.

detail.abstract: This study aims to overcome the structural and interpretative limitations encountered in artificial intelligence causal modelling and explainable AI (XAI) when employing advanced topic modelling techniques (LDA/HDP) alongside traditional grounded theory (GT). It proposes a novel structural variablerelationship modelling framework tailored for complex systems. Employing the Structured Variable-Relationship Modelling (SVRM) methodology, this work integrates the Semantic-Structural Variable Modelling with Policy and Power Analysis (SSVM-PPA) framework. It further incorporates cutting-edge mathematical tools including spectral graph theory, topological data analysis, and information entropy analysis. This comprehensive approach enables an end-to-end modelling system spanning semantic text extraction, causal path modelling, AI graph structure construction, and simulation prediction. Systematic evaluation across 30 texts demonstrates SVRM's superiority over LDA and GT in key metrics: average variable extraction (31.07), structural relationship count (40.13), path significance (0.9), and consistency (0.93), showcasing efficiency, stability, and structural completeness. The research concludes that SVRM not only effectively constructs multi-layered, causally directed variable systems but also broadly adapts to Graph Neural Networks (GNN), Bayesian Networks (BN), and Transformer architectures. This enables embeddable, inferable, and interpretable AI modelling pathways, representing a structural and algorithmic breakthrough in post-empiricism knowledge construction. It provides robust support for strategic simulation, policy intervention, and cognitive modelling.

title: Stable and Profitable Trading Platforms for Smallholder Commodity Supply Chains
affiliations: Stanford University - Institute for Computational and Mathematical Engineering, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Management Science (MS) and Stanford Graduate School of Business

detail.title: Stable and Profitable Trading Platforms for Smallholder Commodity Supply Chains
detail.abstract: Digital platforms that connect smallholder farmers with intermediaries offer a promising path to first-mile traceability and improved livelihoods. Yet such platforms face several challenges. Full disintermediation is often impossible because intermediaries are essential for logistics and deeply embedded in local informal relationship networks; stability is fragile, as farmers and intermediaries may revert to trading through local informal networks if they derive insufficient value on the platform; profit margins are tight; and operations are complex due to fragmentation, scale, heterogeneity, and significant uncertainty about local informal networks. To address these challenges, we develop a flexible model of the platform's joint decisions-matching farmers to intermediaries and setting payments-that captures potential off-platform deviations via local informal networks and enforces stability constraints that preclude them. Deviations are modeled with ambiguity sets that capture the platform's imperfect information and the breadth of intermediaries' relationship networks. We prove structural results and, leveraging them, design exact and approximate branch-and-bound algorithms. We pair a case study based on real data from Indonesia's palm-oil supply chain with a stylized version of the model that we solve analytically, to derive insights regarding the platform's main decisions. Our findings yield several managerial implications. Profitability depends critically on reducing transportation costs and obtaining at least partial data on informal local networks. Payments should be directed primarily to farmers; surprisingly, if intermediaries have larger relationship networks, platforms should increase payments to farmers and decrease payments to intermediaries, which is the most cost-effective way to ensure stability. In dealing with heterogeneous intermediaries, platforms should use efficient (i.e., minimum-cost) matchings unless some intermediaries have extremely large informal relationship networks, in which case they must be prioritized to ensure stability, despite a loss in efficiency.

detail.abstract: This research aims to explore the electrocution risks in Bangladesh and analyze its causes, consequences, and the relevant existing laws. detail.abstract:
This critique looks at the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000 (Republic Act No. 9003). This law was created in response to the tragic Payatas landslide. As a student studying Environmental Waste Management in the Philippines, I examine how RA 9003 presents a good and complete framework. It includes institutions, local governance, community engagement, and environmental health in its design. However, based on audit reports and case studies, I argue that the law's real-world impact falls short. There are gaps in local implementation, uneven infrastructure, such as Material Recovery Facilities and sanitary landfills, and weak enforcement and public awareness. 

By looking at successful examples, like Cebu City, this paper shows that meeting RA 9003's goals needs political will, proper funding, coordination, and skill-building at the local level. I end with specific, student-informed policy recommendations. These include flexible use of funds for staffing, stronger public education, and integrating informal waste collectors. These steps can help turn the law's promise into cleaner streets and a more sustainable future for Filipino communities.

Using robotics statistics, research on tariff incidence, labor market data, and estimates of the prison population, tariffs mainly act as a tax on U.S. consumption and do little to rebuild broad- based, labor-intensive manufacturing. title: Children as Informal Pensions: Intergenerational Insurance and Policy Risks in Africa
affiliations: SBS Swiss Business School

detail.title: Children as Informal Pensions: Intergenerational Insurance and Policy Risks in Africa
detail.abstract: In many African societies, children function as informal pensions, providing financial and caregiving support where formal social protection remains weak or nonexistent. This system, rooted in kinship and cultural ethics such as Ubuntu, has been understood both as an intergenerational investment and as a moral duty. However, demographic transition, youth unemployment, and fragile pension systems threaten its sustainability. While research has focused on fertility decline, dependency ratios, and remittance flows, the ethical and psychosocial dimensions remain underexplored. This paper introduces the Filial Insurance Model (FIM), which synthesizes three logics: investment (parental anticipation of reciprocity), obligation (cultural and moral duty), and sustainability (children's actual capacity to provide). It further develops the concept of the intergenerational insurance trap, where parental expectations collide with children's constrained resources, producing cycles of unmet obligations, relational strain, and poverty transfer. The contribution is threefold: reframing intergenerational support as both economic and ethical; providing a testable framework for future empirical research; and advancing de-risking strategies through hybrid approaches that integrate formal pensions with culturally rooted reciprocity. In doing so, the paper highlights the fragility of reliance on children for old-age security and underscores the urgency of policies that balance cultural traditions with sustainable protections.

title: Enduring Impact, Institutional Resilience and Future Trajectories of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights
affiliations: Institute of the Americas, University College London and University College London

detail.title: Enduring Impact, Institutional Resilience and Future Trajectories of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights
detail.abstract:
This chapter aims to highlight the vital and distinctive role that the IACtHR plays in regional human rights governance, demonstrating its capacity to foster change even under inhospitable political conditions. However, both the Court and the broader Inter-American Human Rights System (IAHRS) face a complex array of challenges; some structural and long-standing, such as concerns over legitimacy, effectiveness, and institutional capacity, and others more immediate, driven by democratic erosion, authoritarian resurgence, and increasing restrictions on civil society. These issues are deeply interconnected, forming a web of pressures that make this a critical moment for the Court’s future relevance. Over more than four decades, the IACtHR has evolved into a fully functioning international tribunal, adjudicating cases, facilitating reparations, and shaping human rights norms. Yet, this progress has been accompanied by persistent obstacles, including chronic underfunding and political backlash, with some governments threatening as well as executing withdrawal in response to adverse rulings. Paradoxically, such tensions underscore both the Court’s enduring significance and the fragility of its mandate in today’s volatile geopolitical climate. Despite its imperfections, the IACtHR remains a crucial mechanism for holding states accountable and empowering individuals and communities to challenge entrenched power structures. The central question is not whether the Court – and human rights more generally – have a future, but how they must evolve to remain effective in a rapidly changing world.

The chapter is structured in three parts. The first part examines the notion of impact beyond compliance, showing how the IACtHR shapes human rights not only through state adherence to rulings but also via its institutional evolution and five key functions that shape regional human rights governance. The second part addresses the complex challenges currently facing the Court, including long-standing structural issues and more immediate political threats, while also identifying sources of resilience that sustain its role. The third and final part looks ahead, outlining three possible future trajectories for the Court – progressive renewal, institutional decline, and a more likely scenario of “muddling through” – and explores how the IACtHR might adapt, innovate, and reaffirm its relevance in an increasingly fraught regional and global context.

detail.abstract: The ellipse perimeter problem, unsolved for over 300 years due to the absence of an elementary closed-form expression, is resolved through a novel discrete computational method rooted in the Tetrahedral-Octahedral (TH-OH) lattice geometry. By rejecting unconstructible transcendental constants (e.g.,) and infinite series, this approach demonstrates that discrete, finite geometry supersedes continuous models, shattering the foundation of classical computational geometry.

The sample size is 200 from the Sri Lanka Navy officers. This is a quantitative study. The unit of analysis is individual, and this cross-sectional study was completed in a non-contrived setting with minimal interference by the researcher. This study employs a partial least squares (PLS) regression model within the Smart PLS 4.0 software framework to investigate the underlying objectives. The primary focus entails a meticulous examination of the measurement model, ensuring the robustness of the questionnaire through a thorough assessment of reliability and validity. title: AI Actionability Over Interpretability

detail.title: AI Actionability Over Interpretability
detail.abstract: Traditional approaches to model risk management emphasize interpretability--understanding how models generate outputs--as a foundation for trust and governance. This paper argues that interpretability, while valuable, is insufficient for effective risk management of generative AI systems. Unlike conventional models that can be decomposed into discrete, understandable components, large language models exhibit emergent behavior arising from complex parameter interactions. Moreover, enterprise AI deployments increasingly involve multiple systems including retrieval-augmented generation, guardrails, and agents that further complicate interpretability efforts. We propose prioritizing actionability over interpretability--ensuring that AI reasoning processes are sufficiently observable to enable timely diagnosis and remediation when failures occur. This approach includes techniques such as Chain-of-Thought reasoning, Chain-of-Prompts scaffolding, and agentic tracing to create structured observability into AI decision-making processes. While these methods currently face limitations and vulnerabilities, they provide a more practical foundation for building trust in AI systems than interpretability alone. Actionability through observability offers financial institutions and regulators a viable path for responsible AI deployment at scale, potentially warranting updates to existing model risk management frameworks, such as SR 11-7.

title: Deglobalisation or Reglobalisation? A Macroperspective on the Reemergence of the Global Economy

detail.title: Deglobalisation or Reglobalisation? A Macroperspective on the Reemergence of the Global Economy
detail.abstract: Recent geopolitical and economic shocks, such as the rise of protectionist trade policies, Brexit, and the Russia-Ukraine conflict, have shaken the foundation of globalisation. While often invisible, some borders have become more porous, while others have become less so. The deglobalisation hypothesis is gaining traction in response to these shocks. This paper attempts to debunk this hypothesis by proposing a counterbalancing reglobalisation hypothesis. Rather than representing a decline in globalisation, the global economy is transforming towards a more strategically realigned system. Through an analysis of trends in trade flows, foreign direct investment, and migration, this paper argues that the global economy is undergoing a structural adjustment, marked by increasing regionalisation and technological advancement. The paper identifies a shift in the global economic order and a transfer of political power from the West to the East driven by political realignment, relocation of trade and investment, restrategising, and remigration. It concludes that reglobalisation offers a more comprehensive framework for understanding regional transformations and their role in shaping the future of globalisation. Recommendations for future research are offered.

title: Beyond Duality: Exploring "Nothingness" in the Advaita Vedānta and the Madhyamaka Traditions of Indian Buddhism
affiliations: Al Seeb Vocational College Muscat Oman

detail.title: Beyond Duality: Exploring "Nothingness" in the Advaita Vedānta and the Madhyamaka Traditions of Indian Buddhism
detail.abstract: This article explores the concept of "nothingness" in the Advaita Vedānta and Madhyamaka traditions of Indian Buddhism, analysing their convergences, divergences, and broader implications within Indian philosophical traditions. Both systems emphasize the transcendence of duality and the limitations of ordinary perception in realizing ultimate truth. For Advaita Vedānta, Brahman-the singular, eternal essence-is the sole reality, with the phenomenal world regarded as an illusion (māyā). Liberation arises through self-realization, where one recognizes the unity of self (atman) and Brahman. Conversely, Madhyamaka Buddhism denies the existence of any inherent essence, positing emptiness (Śūnyatā) as the nature of all phenomena. Liberation in this framework involves the cessation of clinging and the realization of interdependence. The article contextualizes these philosophies within their socio-cultural milieus, revealing how their metaphysical claims respond to existential and ethical concerns. While Advaita seeks to unify diversity through non-dualism, Madhyamaka challenges rigid constructs, emphasizing relational existence. Comparative analysis highlights shared principles, such as the critique of egobased delusion and the transformative power of wisdom, alongside distinct soteriological paths rooted in their metaphysical differences. By engaging with these traditions, the article not only underscores their philosophical richness, but also explores their relevance to contemporary issues, including existential anxiety and ethical dilemmas.

detail.title: Pricing Strategies in Online Education
detail.abstract: What is the optimal pricing strategy in an online education context? In this paper, we propose three pricing strategies for online education: single upfront pricing, upfront pricing combined with a certification fee, and upfront pricing combined with cashback. We develop a game-theoretical framework to explore the impact of these pricing strategies on user learning and purchasing behaviors, and we discuss which is optimal under different circumstances. Within this framework, we capture the unique characteristics of online education products and online learners by considering cost uncertainty and users' present-biased preferences. Our findings suggest that the cashback strategy is optimal when the market anticipates that the required effort cost will be high relative to the benefits earned, whereas the certification strategy is optimal when the market expects the effort cost to be low relative to the benefits gained.

detail.title: The Cost of Inaccessibility: Retail Discrimination and Mobility-Constrained Consumers
detail.abstract: This study investigates whether individuals with mobility-related health conditions face systematic disadvantages in retail pricing, both in physical stores and on online platforms. While price discrimination is a common feature of modern markets, limited attention has been paid to how physical mobility constraints may affect consumers' ability to access lower prices or respond to promotions. Using matched observational data from the NielsenIQ and the Open E-Commerce dataset, we compare purchasing behavior and price outcomes between consumers with and without mobility-related health conditions. We find that mobility-constrained individuals pay modestly higher prices in physical stores and face even larger price disparities in online purchases, particularly among wheelchair users. Our findings highlight mobility as an underexamined axis of vulnerability in consumer markets. The results have implications for the design of retail pricing systems and digital platforms, as well as for policy efforts aimed at improving equity in access to essential goods.

title: Shock Doctrine in the Life Sciences - When Fear Overwhelms Facts

detail.title: Shock Doctrine in the Life Sciences - When Fear Overwhelms Facts
detail.abstract: Emerging biotechnologies have repeatedly triggered public alarms that exceed empirical evidence of risk. From recombinant DNA and genetically modified crops to synthetic cells, AI-enabled drug design, and the speculative creation of “mirror life,” the life sciences have cycled through periods of dramatic warnings followed by measured scientific progress. This essay examines how worst-case narratives—what Naomi Klein termed the “Shock Doctrine”—have shaped governance by privileging hypothetical catastrophes over demonstrated benefits. Historical case studies and contemporary debates illustrate how fear-driven policy can suppress innovation, distort public trust, and impose ethical costs as serious as the risks it seeks to avoid. Recombinant DNA research produced insulin rather than pandemics, and genetically modified crops improved yields without the ecological collapses that were forecast. Current claims that AI or mirror life inevitably pose existential threats risk repeating this cycle. A proportional, evidence-based approach to biotechnology risk assessment is recommended—one that safeguards against genuine hazards while avoiding speculative extremes. Such a framework can sustain both innovation and safety, resisting the paralysis that results when fear overwhelms fact.

detail.title: The Time-Varying Salience Premium: Is it there?
detail.abstract: We examine whether the abnormal return of a salience-based long-short portfolio varies over time. To answer this question, our paper proposes a new semiparametric conditional factor model. This model lets alpha (abnormal return) follow a highly general form, unlike existing studies that impose specific parametric constraints.​ We use a two-step profile estimation method on monthly data from 1967 to 2024. Our results show that the salience premium has strong time variation after controlling for common risk factors. For the equal weighted salience portfolio, the abnormal return is statistically significant in most of our sample period, except for a short window around the COVID-19 pandemic.​ We also conduct nonparametric uniform tests and reject the null hypothesis that long-run abnormal returns are either zero or constant. The observed variation in the salience premium is driven by time changes in lottery preference, risk appetite, investor sentiment, and market conditions.​ However, the salience premium’s significance depends heavily on how the salience portfolio is constructed. For value-weighted salience portfolios, the premium is only significant before 1985.

detail.abstract: We analyze a market-wide panel dataset on retail options trading from India, a market with an 80% share in option contracts traded worldwide. Retail traders both concentrated in and dominate index options trading. They exhibit short-term speculative behavior with significant day trading, shortduration directional bets especially as options converge to 0DTE and make significant losses. detail.abstract: As India aspires to transition into a developed economy by 2047, this paper examines key economic indicators that highlight the disparities between India and more developed nations, particularly the United States and the United Kingdom. Utilizing data from various reputable sources, the analysis explores Gross National Income, per capita income, unemployment rates, and the Human Development Index, among other factors. In 2024, India's Gross National Income and per capita income are significantly lower than those of its developed counterparts, indicating substantial challenges ahead. The paper also highlights critical areas such as inflation rates, industrial productivity, agricultural contributions to GDP, and educational attainment, which collectively underscore the necessity for strategic economic reforms and targeted social policies. Additionally, the analysis addresses the implications of demographic trends and life expectancy disparities, reflecting on the importance of improving healthcare access and quality of life. The findings reveal that while India demonstrates considerable growth potential, achieving its developmental goals requires a unified effort to enhance economic resilience, foster social equity, and promote sustainable growth along with realistic women empowerment. This study aims to provide insights into the critical pathways India must undertake to realize its vision of becoming a developed nation by 2047.

detail.abstract: Natural resources (land, water, soils, and natural vegetation) are vital for sustaining crop production and enabling adaptation to climate change. Using the global land-use model MAgPIE, we evaluate current and future availability of these resources across global crop-producing regions under three socioeconomic and climate scenarios. These trends are linked to the expansion and intensification of cropland, driven by increasing income and demand for food and bioenergy. Our results underscore the pressing need to integrate sustainability and resilience into agricultural development, thereby safeguarding food security and ecosystems amid global change.

detail.abstract: The large-scale destruction of industrial, energy and infrastructure facilities during the war has a destructive impact on social development and the progress of the business sector. The European integration concept of Ukraine's postwar recovery envisages active reconstruction of cities based on sustainable development. The article aims to analyse the scale of infrastructure destruction in Ukraine during the war and its impact on sustainable urban development. The study identifies potential risks for the urban development strategy caused by infrastructure destruction. The system of management of reconstruction projects and the state of coordination of management activities in this aspect are investigated. The need to transfer modern approaches generally accepted in the international community to upgrade local management structures for urban development is determined. The necessity of improving the regulatory framework in this aspect is substantiated. The potential of the energy security system against the background of the risks of damage to urban infrastructure is investigated. The sectoral objectives included in Goal 11 of the General Strategy for Sustainable Development-Sustainable Development of Cities and Communities-are analysed. It is proved that large-scale destruction of infrastructure, including critical infrastructure, causes instability in socioeconomic development, destroys the environment, and worsens the investment climate. detail.abstract: This paper introduces stackdid, a new, community-contributed Stata command that makes implementing stacked difference-indifferences regressions remarkably straightforward. stackdid handles all the complexity of restructuring panel data into "stacks" of "cohorts" centered on treatment events and performs the specified regression. It integrates seamlessly with existing high-dimensional fixed effects estimators and supports both linear and Poisson specifications, allowing researchers to adapt their preferred specifications to the stacked framework with ease. stackdid provides an assortment of options enabling precise model specification and robustness analysis. This command provides researchers with an accessible, practical tool for implementing the stacked difference-indifferences methodology, contributing to the growing toolkit for robust causal inference with differential treatment timing.

detail.abstract: In this paper, the author critically evaluates the 30-year interval between 1993-2023 by analysing the evidence found in the literature on conventions at the macro-level. The paper critiques the so-called rules-based approach of contemporary policy choice and questions the direction of its intended course. The paper uses the governance framework taken from the ISSB's Disclosure and Non-Financial Reporting approach to illustrate, comparatively, and then highlights how the Taylor model of inflation targeting creates uncertainty, due partly to an inherent adherence by policymakers to prescriptive rules (Orphanides, 2001). This paper concludes by attempting to illustrate how by not internalising a risk-based approach (in favour of a rulesbased approach), UK and US monetary policy conventions have underestimated an indirect cause of inflationary regimes.

detail.abstract: This study analyzes the impact of technological change on job satisfaction of women garment workers in Bangladesh. A set of job satisfaction variables was developed from the Technological Change Survey (Slem and Levi, 1995). The specific relationship between job satisfaction and the overall satisfaction shows that fair pay, task significance, bureaucracy, conflicts, and information sharing are significantly related. Task significance and information sharing are positively related to the overall impact. Fair pay, bureaucracy and conflicts are negatively and significantly related to the overall impact.

title: The Medieval Origins of Spousal Consent
affiliations: University of Mississippi - Department of Economics and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Medieval Origins of Spousal Consent
detail.abstract: This paper examines the medieval origins of spousal consent, the norm requiring that marriages be contracted willingly and free from pressure from third parties. We argue that this norm resulted from the Catholic Church's consolidation of legal authority over marriage in the 11th-12th centuries. Committed doctrinally to the belief that marriages could not be dissolved and that remarriage was therefore impermissible (i.e., marriage indissolubility), the Church was compelled to enforce high consent requirements to the formation of new unions. Using a simple theoretical model, we show that the Church's optimal level of spousal consent is higher when remarriage is not allowed. Higher consent requirements mitigate the negative effect of indissolubility on the number of marriages contracted. The development of a theory of spousal consent marked a sharp break from pre-Christian practice, which gave parents substantial control over the choice of spouse. It also contrasted with Eastern Orthodoxy and Protestantism, both of which permitted remarriage after divorce. Our analysis suggests that the Church's insistence on free consent was a necessary institutional complement to its unique stance on indissolubility, shaping marriage law and family structure in ways that reverberated throughout European history.

title: Violence at School
affiliations: School of Government, Pontificia Universidad Catolica, Pontificia Universidad Catolica de Chile and World Bank

detail.title: Violence at School

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper estimates the impact of violence perpetrated by peers and school staff on student victims. Leveraging unique administrative data from Chile that links reports of school violence to individual educational records, we address longstanding data limitations that have constrained empirical research on this issue. Using a matched difference-in-differences design, we find that exposure to school violence has persistent negative effects: absenteeism increases by 4664\%, grade retention rates double, and both grades and test scores decline significantly, with impacts lasting up to four years. In the longer term, victims are substantially less likely to graduate from high school or enroll in university, with violence perpetrated by adults having more severe consequences than peer violence. Complementary survey evidence reveals that reported incidents are associated with increased perceptions of violence and discrimination, as well as decreases in school belonging and teacher expectations. While these psychological and perceptual effects tend to fade after one year, the adverse educational consequences persist, underscoring how brief traumatic experiences can lead to long-lasting educational disadvantages.

detail.abstract: Procedural rights in the tax administration deal with the rules and procedures that help citizens and businesses comply with their tax obligations to the state. ―The tax administration system consists of state bodies that have the right to collect revenues for the budget, and a set of rules and regulations that govern the tax procedure in the country‖ (Temchyshyna, 2022, p. 206). This study aims to treat the procedural rights in tax administration in theoretical aspects and comparative aspects, through Balkan countries. The research model was based on qualitative research, based on normative method, comparative method, analytic method, and descriptive method, all of these methods based on credible sources, like legal acts, scientific papers, official reports from official bodies, and non-government organizations. Furthermore, this study aims to make a review analysis of the procedural rights that are missing in the tax administrative legislation system in Kosovo, identify and treat the theoretical aspects of procedural rights of taxpayers in tax administration in general, and analyze challenges of tax administration in actuality and general. The main findings of the study show that the Tax Administration of Kosovo has made great progress by modernizing itself and simplifying its procedures for tax-paying citizens.

title: There Is Nothing We Can Do" For Some And "I Can Do Everything" For Others: AI Revolution, Perceived Behavioral Control Across Social Classes in the D.R.Congo
affiliations: Université Libre des Pays des Grands Lacs

detail.title: There Is Nothing We Can Do" For Some And "I Can Do Everything" For Others: AI Revolution, Perceived Behavioral Control Across Social Classes in the D.R.Congo
detail.abstract: Anticipating disruptive technologies often reveals deep social divides in how individuals interpret change. This paper examines the psychological consequences of imagining an Artificial Intelligence (AI) revolution in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), with particular attention to perceived behavioral control (PBC). Drawing on the Theory of Planned Behavior, we conceptualize PBC through two key dimensions: self-efficacy and locus of control. Using a randomized experimental design with treatment, placebo, and control conditions, participants were primed with narratives of AI disruption, after which shifts in their sense of agency were measured. Findings indicate that AI primes significantly reduced perceptions of controllability, especially among disadvantaged groups, while self-efficacy remained largely stable. Conversely, individuals with relative advantages, proxied by car ownership and male gender, demonstrated resilience, and in certain cases even a rebound effect, suggesting that access to material and symbolic resources protects against the disempowering effects of disruptive change. These results underscore a critical psychological cleavage: whereas advantaged participants are inclined to view AI as opportunity, marginalized participants experience it as an uncontrollable threat. The study contributes to debates on inequality, perceived behavioral control, and technology adoption by revealing how social class moderates psychological responses to anticipated technological transformations. Policy implications emphasize that reducing inequality requires not only digital infrastructure and skill-building, but also the cultivation of psychological resources such as Locus of control, inclusion, and self-efficacy to mitigate the risk of AI amplifying existing divides.

detail.abstract:
This paper presents a research approach on anticipatory democracy which addresses the methodology for computing the “desirable futures”, a basic concept in Anticipatory Democracy studies (Bezolt, 1978, 2010). The paper elaborates on the build-up of a computational and simulation model for computing the desirable future in anticipatory social-political systems. The research is aimed for the study of hybrid social-political systems defined as anticipatory systems and can be further developed for virtual and immersive social-political anticipatory systems.

This paper provides a anticipatory democracy research approach on achieving desirable futures (aspirational futures) in a social-political system defined as a hybrid environment, where the term ‘hybrid environment’ defines a social-political environment which includes both physical and virtual space and time dimensions, and the term ‘anticipatory system’ is the definition of a complex social-political system with an internal model of itself which employs it for achieving reflexivity and computing the future state(s) (Rosen 1985, p.341; Dubois, 1998a, b; Leydesdorff and Dubois, 2004; Dubois, 2020).

The approach reported in this paper is a research methodology approach based on early theory and methodology in (i) modelling and simulation of political culture by value mappings (Voinea, 2021a, b; 2022a, b), and (ii) mathematical and computational modelling of anticipatory systems (Dubois, 1998a, b; Dubois and Resconi, 1993; Dubois, 2001).  The research approach on the modelling of a hybrid social-political anticipatory system in this paper is inspired by the theories on time and spatialization of time from classic and contemporary film theory and cinematography (Panofsky, 1934/1947; Deleuze, 1985/1989; Elsaesser, 2009). Filmmaking can teach us two lessons about how to employ space and time in order to explain and provide for a desirable future state of an evolving complex social-political environment (Dunat, 2022; Yaffe, 2003; Deleuze, 1985/1989; Bluestone, 1961). The approach in this paper adapts the concepts of ‘time’ and ‘space’ in film theory to the simulation and computation of a anticipatory system for achieving the desirable future state of the system. The paper suggests a methodology which employs multiple space locations and time segments for the study of desirable futures in an experimental scenario of mass participation to political protests in hybrid social-political environments.

This research approach proves relevant for the research on hybrid, virtual and immersive anticipatory systems in areas with high emotional intensity and stress, like healthcare, financial markets, and art industries with high emotional and cultural impact like movie industry. It addresses research issues like meaning co-creation, value co-creation, and design of aspirational futures in social and political environments.

Our approach emphasizes a difference from the classic mathematical and computational model of anticipatory systems: it brings a multiple space and time segments approach in order to operationalize the participation of individuals in mass political protests in hybrid social-political environments. Our approach adapts concepts and theories about time and space from film theory such that the multiple space and time dimensions representing the many individuals’ participation in political phenomena could be appropriately used in the definition, description and operationalization of hybrid social-political systems defined as anticipatory systems. The approach has been employed for the computation of desirable futures in a Case Study on Romanian phenomena of political regime change in 1989 by employing visual and content analysis of data extracted from the 1989 Romanian Anti-Communism Revolution TV-Streaming on Romanian National Television channel.

title: The Impact of EAC Customs Union On Rwanda’s Customs Revenues
affiliations: National University of Rwanda

detail.title: The Impact of EAC Customs Union On Rwanda’s Customs Revenues

contentType.other: Thesis for obtaining a Mater's degree

detail.abstract:
This study was carried out to find out the impact of EAC Customs Union on Rwanda’s customs revenues.

The general objective of this study was to verify the impact of EAC Customs Union on Rwanda’s customs revenues, while the specific objectives were to identify the share of tariffs in the Government revenues and to find out ways Rwandan government shall use to find and/or mobilize new resources to compensate the tariff revenue losses due to EAC Customs Union.

The study used a convenience sampling method to select customs offices from which sample individuals would be got after determining a sample size of 95 customs offices staffs using simple random sampling technique where necessary.

To collect the necessary data both primary and secondary sources were used namely questionnaire and documentary study techniques and collected data have been analyzed using SPSS (Statistical Package for Social Sciences).

Research findings revealed that, customs revenues have a great share in the total government tax revenue, and this share has decreased after the Rwanda join to the EAC Customs Union. This is to indicate that Rwanda suffered a loss in customs revenue. Therefore, the null hypothesis of this research which stated that the East African Community Customs Union has a negative impact on Rwanda’s customs revenues was not rejected.

Even though the means by which the Rwandan government will use to compensate the loss in revenue were found out, the impact still persists.

The ways to cover the revenue loss faced by Rwanda due to the implementation of EAC Customs Union were recommended.

Finally, the researcher recommended to carry out a further research on the impact of EAC Customs Union on Partner States’ customs revenues.

title: Building Resilience, Ethics, and Emotional Skills in Children: A Guide for Educators and Parents
affiliations: Founder, SHADOW

detail.title: Building Resilience, Ethics, and Emotional Skills in Children: A Guide for Educators and Parents
detail.abstract: Children's mental health and social-emotional well-being are critical global priorities. Recent data show that roughly one in seven adolescents experience significant mental health conditions (World Health Organization, 2025). Yet many primary schools, especially in low-resource contexts, lack structured programs to foster resilience, empathy, and ethical behavior. For example, UNICEF reports that Bangladesh has begun integrating mental health support into the national curriculum (United Nations Children's Fund [UNICEF], 2025), yet educators often still lack formal SEL training (Reza, 2024). This mixed-methods study surveyed primary students (ages 6-11) in Bangladesh, along with their teachers and parents, to identify gaps in SEL awareness and practices. The study found that adults recognize the importance of social-emotional learning but often feel unprepared, while children commonly struggled with anger management, empathy, and understanding fairness. The study proposes a dual-level intervention framework. The first level is a training curriculum for teachers and parents, covering child development, resilience-building, emotional coaching, and ethical reasoning. The second level is an age-appropriate SEL roadmap for students in Classes 1-5, using games, role-play, and stories to build emotional vocabulary and moral skills step by step. Together, these modules aim to strengthen children's coping strategies, improve classroom and home environments, and promote children's long-term well-being.

title: When Do Consumers Lose from Variable Electricity Pricing?
affiliations: , Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems

detail.title: When Do Consumers Lose from Variable Electricity Pricing?
detail.abstract:
Time-varying electricity pricing better reflects the varying cost of electricity compared to flat-rate pricing. Variations between peak and off-peak costs are increasing due to weather variation, renewable intermittency, and increasing electrification of demand. Empirical and theoretical studies suggest that variable pricing can lower electricity supply costs and reduce grid stress. However, the distributional impacts, particularly on low-income consumers, remain understudied. This paper develops a theoretical framework to analyze how consume heterogeneity affects welfare outcomes when electricity markets transition from flat-rate to time-varying pricing, considering realistic assumptions about heterogeneous consumer demand, supply costs, and utility losses from unmet consumption.

We derive sufficient conditions for identifying when consumers lose utility from pricing reforms and compare welfare effects across consumer types. Our findings reveal that consumer vulnerability depends on the interaction of consumption timing, demand flexibility capabilities, and price sensitivity levels. Consumers with high peak-period consumption and inflexible demand, characteristics often associated with low-income households, are most vulnerable to welfare losses. Critically, we demonstrate that demand flexibility provides welfare protection only when coincident with large price changes, a condition more easily met by higher-income consumers in most empirical studies. Our equilibrium analysis reveals that aggregate flexibility patterns generate spillover effects through pricing mechanisms, with peak periods experiencing greater price changes when they have less aggregate flexibility, potentially concentrating larger price increases among vulnerable populations that have a limited ability to respond. These findings suggest that variable pricing policies designed to support clean energy transitions risk exacerbating energy inequality unless accompanied by targeted policies ensuring equitable access to demand response capabilities and pricing benefits.

title: Commercial Christmas Cheer: The Reestablishment and Proliferation of Christmas Markets in Post-World War II Germany (1945–2020)
affiliations: Charles Sturt University - Gulbali Institute for Agriculture, Water and Environment, Charles Sturt University

detail.title: Commercial Christmas Cheer: The Reestablishment and Proliferation of Christmas Markets in Post-World War II Germany (1945–2020)
detail.abstract: Originating in the Middle Ages as venues for purchasing supplies and goods in preparation of the midwinter season, Christmas markets have morphed into a multi-sensory experiential events and social venues. Christmas markets have been publicised as the quintessential event in Germany leading up to Christmas, with the over 2000 locations attracting large numbers of local, domestic and international visitors. Yet, after World War I such markets were becoming obsolete, only to be revived by Nazi politicians in the late 1930s. Drawing on a dataset of dates of commencement or more than 1000 German communities specifically compiled for this study, this paper traces the history of the Christmas markets from the immediate post-World War II period until the COVID-19 ('Corona') pandemic of 2020 which saw a temporary cessation of all markets. The paper argues that these markets played an important role during the period of postwar austerity and the early economic recovery, but that thereafter many became an anachronism. Only the wave of nostalgia that followed the oil shock of 1973 and the period of social and economic change of the early 1970s saw a resurgence and rapid expansion of Christmas markets that gradually grew into the social, experiential phenomenon that we know today.

title: Climate Projections Affect Restoration Priorities: Application to Brazilian Forests
affiliations: American University of Armenia

detail.title: Climate Projections Affect Restoration Priorities: Application to Brazilian Forests
detail.abstract: While ecological dynamics have been shown to affect restoration targeting decisions, the impact of climate change on the economic value of restoration remains less explored. Climate change can be expected to affect both the benefits and costs of a particular restoration project, through changing crop yields, vegetation, and urbanization, among other factors, potentially leading to abandonment of sites or forgone opportunity. Here, we first present a framework for understanding the effect of projected changes on the economic value of a restoration project. We then apply the model to an empirical context of interest: habitat restoration via forest replanting in Brazil, focusing on the implications of two specific climate projections: changing crop yields and changing forest cover habitat. We find that active restoration would yield net benefits in a majority of grid cells across the country, monetizing benefits of restored lands by considering habitat value alone, yet that integrating projections of conditions in 2050 yields greater expected benefits than present conditions would suggest, with an increase in the median grid cell of 41 percent and significant spatial variation. Our results illustrate the importance of accounting for projected changes in conditions in restoration planning, and support for the economic value of wide-scale restoration programs which provide biodiversity protection.

detail.abstract: In this paper we present a theory which purports to explain why competition regulators may choose to sacrifice decision accuracy, adopting pessimistic beliefs about firms' conduct-beliefs that overestimate the likelihood of firm infringement and underestimate non-infringement-and ignoring economic evidence contradicting those beliefs. Unlike models where beliefs are assumed exogenous, here beliefs are treated as endogenous and potentially shaped by institutional, personal, or contextual factors. In a nutshell, we argue that agencies' skepticism is not the result of mis-information, but rather is driven by cognitive dissonance, reinforced by cultural capture, stereotypical thinking, and viral political narratives: morality tales and conspiracy theories. Surprisingly, perhaps, their skepticism may prove consumer and total welfare increasing, though at the cost of accuracy and at the expense of compliant firms.

title: Are Highways Conduits or Barriers for Urban Travelers? A Welfare Analysis Using Smartphone Data

detail.title: Are Highways Conduits or Barriers for Urban Travelers? A Welfare Analysis Using Smartphone Data
detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the impact of highways on intracity travel using granular smartphone GPS data. I find that urban highways act as barriers to travel: conditional on travel time, destinations reached by crossing highways are 24.9% less likely to be chosen, and those reached by using highways are 23.5% less likely. The impacts are stronger for short, consumption trips and weaker for commuting. Using a quantitative urban model that integrates both work and consumption travel, I evaluate the welfare effects of two counterfactual highway systems that remove the estimated disamenities. Both scenarios yield welfare gains of at least 9%. These gains arise from improved access to urban amenities, which strengthens agglomeration as population, employment, and consumption opportunities shift from suburban to urban centers. This reallocation increases urban amenities but also raises urban land prices, while generating opposite effects in suburban areas. Decomposition shows that amenity improvements from consumption travel account for up to 72% of the total welfare gain, highlighting the contribution of this mechanism.

title: Central Bank Communication and Biodiversity

detail.title: Central Bank Communication and Biodiversity
detail.abstract: Biodiversity loss has been identified as a driver of systemic financial risk, yet its integration into supervisory frameworks and central bank agendas remains nascent. This paper provides the first analysis of how biodiversity is addressed in central bank communication, drawing on over 11,000 speeches in the Bank for International Settlements database between 2012 and 2024. Using a hybrid natural language processing approach that combines dictionary filtering and semantic similarity scoring, I identify 141 biodiversity-related speeches, of which only 19 place biodiversity at the core of the discussion.The analysis reveals several key findings. First, biodiversity is largely absent from central bank discourse, appearing in less than 2% of speeches and overwhelmingly framed through climate-related risks. Second, when mentioned explicitly, recommendations remain limited to exploratory calls for improved data, disclosure, and risk metrics, without operational integration into supervisory tools. Third, discourse is highly uneven across jurisdictions, concentrated in a few European central banks, while most authorities remain silent.These findings point to a significant blind spot in financial stability agendas: despite ever-growing evidence that biodiversity loss may generate systemic risks comparable to climate change, the majority of central banks have yet to recognize biodiversity as a distinct and material source of financial vulnerability in their communication.

detail.abstract: This research explores how behavioral economics theories, particularly the Decoy Effect, can be applied to real-life sales strategies within a high school setting. Conducted at Catlin Gabel School, the experiment tested merchandise pricing strategies by introducing a decoy item that aimed to dominate students' purchasing behavior. Sales data showed a significant increase from 23% to 78% in target purchases when the decoy was present. To quantify this effect, a profit function model was developed using key variables: original purchase probability (q₀), adjusted probability under influence (q₁), and decoy detection probability (δ). The findings highlight how consumer choices can be shaped by pricing structures and support the use of behavioral economics in school-based or small business sales planning. Limitations of decoy effect and future applications are discussed.

detail.abstract: The study investigates the prevalence of food insecurity, its determinants and the association of food insecurity with governance and socioeconomic factors in Nigeria. The study used secondary data for the period 1999 to 2018. The main method of analysis used for the work is Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL). The result of the ARDL bound testing shows that the null hypothesis of no cointegration is rejected. title: Towards Comprehensive Medical Leave Legislation: Ensuring Health Rights in Bangladeshi Workplaces

detail.title: Towards Comprehensive Medical Leave Legislation: Ensuring Health Rights in Bangladeshi Workplaces
detail.abstract: The right to health is a cornerstone of human dignity and productivity. However, in Bangladesh, workplace medical leave is still largely treated as a privilege rather than a statutory entitlement. While the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006, provides for limited sick leave, its scope remains confined to industrial workers, excluding the majority of professionals in education, services, and non-governmental sectors. This paper critically examines the absence of a comprehensive legal framework on medical leave in Bangladesh. Drawing on International Labour Organization (ILO) conventions, constitutional provisions, and comparative jurisprudence, it argues for immediate legislative reform. Particular attention is paid to environmental and occupational health challenges, socioeconomic implications, and the binding nature of Bangladesh's international commitments under instruments such as the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR). Ultimately, the paper calls for the recognition of medical leave as a legally enforceable right for all workers, thereby advancing justice, health, and sustainable development.

title: Reassessing the Strength of Industrial Banks: Evidence, Trends, and Policy Implications
affiliations: University of Utah - David Eccles School of Business, University of Utah - David Eccles School of Business and Northeastern University

detail.title: Reassessing the Strength of Industrial Banks: Evidence, Trends, and Policy Implications

declarations.funderStatement: Stena Center for Financial Technology provided funding for the project.

detail.abstract: Industrial banks (IB) are state-chartered, FDIC-insured institutions that commercial or financial parents may own, and they occupy a distinctive niche in the U.S. banking system. We document that IBs differ from other FDIC-insured banks along three core margins: (i) ownership and supervision (CALMA/PCA commitments that contractually obligate parents to act as sources of strength), (ii) business models (specialized, often nationally distributed lending with heavy use of brokered deposits), and (iii) performance and resilience. From 2000 to 2025, we demonstrate that IBs-especially those with commercial parents-exhibit persistently higher ROA/ROE and stronger capitalization than other banks. Critically, this exists even during the Global Financial Crisis and the COVID-19 shock. IB funding relies disproportionately on (insured) brokered deposits and higher capitalization. As a result, IB failures are rare and small in aggregate relative to the broader system. IBs have niche business models that lead them to decrease market concentration and enable them to increase product innovation. Their market segments focus on specialized and underserved segments, often using information advantages from their parent company. We discuss the policy tradeoffs of layering additional regulation onto a framework in which FDIC/state oversight already mirrors that of comparable banks. We find little evidence that restrictions on commercial ownership would deliver stability benefits, but that they could increase compliance and innovation costs.

title: Effect of Rice Husk and Bamboo Biochar on Soil Compaction in Paddy Fields under Varying Moisture Conditions

detail.title: Effect of Rice Husk and Bamboo Biochar on Soil Compaction in Paddy Fields under Varying Moisture Conditions

publicationDetails.detailsText: Mediterranean Journal of Basic and Applied Sciences, volume 09, issue 03, 2025[10.46382/MJBAS.2025.9307]

detail.abstract: Soil compaction impacts the physical quality of paddy fields by hindering water infiltration, limiting aeration, and stunting root growth. The use of biochar has emerged as a promising approach to mitigate soil compaction and improve soil structure. This study aimed to investigate the effects of rice husk and petung bamboo biochar on soil compaction at different moisture levels. Laboratory assays employing standard compaction tests of soils were performed, and the resulting data were subjected to quadratic regression analysis. Both rice husk and petung bamboo biochars showed a quadratic relationship between soil moisture and compaction with R² values of 0.8512 and 0.9913, respectively. Also, rice husk biochar lowered soil compaction so that bulk density decreased from 1.393937 g.cm⁻³ at 27%(w/w) moisture to 1.2006 g.cm⁻³ at 41% (w/w) moisture. Meanwhile, soil with petung bamboo biochar reached a maximum bulk density of 1.3806 g.cm⁻³ at 36% (w/w) moisture and was stable at higher moistures. The effectiveness of biochars in reducing soil compaction is attributed to their physical properties such as porosity and density. From the results, it is suggested that the application of rice husk biochar effectively improves paddy field soil structure and supports sustainable agriculture practices.

title: The Proliferation of Unilateral Trade Measures and the Crisis of the Multilateral Trading System
affiliations: NingboTech University - School of Law

detail.title: The Proliferation of Unilateral Trade Measures and the Crisis of the Multilateral Trading System
detail.abstract: Following President Trump's assumption of office at the start of the year, he introduced a series of tariff measures. These unilateral trade actions, especially the reciprocal tariffs, could have profound and far-reaching consequences, potentially undermining the very foundations of the multilateral trading system. This is due to their direct challenge to the Most-Favored-Nation (MFN) principle, a cornerstone of the World Trade Organization (WTO). Additionally, the unilateral trade measures imposed by the United States have triggered follow-up actions from other nations, resulting in reciprocal countermeasures. It is critical to determine how to respond to reciprocal tariffs in a manner that preserves the integrity of the multilateral trading system. Special attention must be given to the creation of a complex network of bilateral agreements, formed through bilateral consultations after the implementation of US reciprocal tariffs, which may indirectly weaken the multilateral framework.

detail.title: The Role of Financial Traders for Price Responses to Shocks in the Commodity Futures Markets
detail.abstract: I investigate the conditions under which financial traders amplify price responses to significant spot market price changes in 13 agricultural commodity futures markets. Financial traders dampen price changes during the Russia-Ukraine war but amplify them during the Global Financial Crisis. However, this mitigating effect depends on the market share of financial traders: as their market share grows, the mitigation effect weakens and eventually reverses, leading to amplified price changes. According to hedging pressure theory, financial traders help dampen price changes by providing liquidity to commercial hedgers in exchange for earning a risk premium. By identifying when they cease to act as liquidity providers, I offer robust support for the hypothesis that financial traders may amplify price changes under specific conditions.
