detail.abstract: This paper proposes a multicausal framework to explain the transition from critical skepticism to identity-based denialism, positioning confirmation bias (CB) as the central organizing axis. The framework argues that CB does not operate in isolation but as a cross-level mechanism that integrates biological, cognitive, relational, and structural factors. These include behavioral genetics, epigenetics, immunogenetics, attributional and cognitive styles, epistemic subcultures, homophily, symbolic belonging, and pro-engagement algorithms. The model reframes denialism, or organized cognitive resistance, not as a simple information deficit but as a practice of identity and belonging, which accounts for its persistence in the face of contradictory evidence. The paper derives core and exploratory hypotheses and outlines their operationalization through psychometric scales, experimental paradigms, digital trace analyses, and biomarkers, with an emphasis on longitudinal designs and confounding control. The implications of this research are organized across several key areas: education (metacognitive literacy), public policy (algorithmic transparency and auditing), science (openness and self-critique), organizational management (preventing epistemic closure), and interdisciplinarity. The analysis concludes that displacing confirmation bias from its dominant role is a necessary condition for restoring genuinely open critical thinking, which is indispensable for countering the consolidation of denialist movements in polarized, platform-mediated publics.

title: WTO Trade Dispute Mechanism Is More Power-Based Than Rule-Based

detail.title: WTO Trade Dispute Mechanism Is More Power-Based Than Rule-Based
detail.abstract: The World Trade Organization (WTO) dispute settlement mechanism was designed to provide a rule-based framework for resolving international trade conflicts, ensuring fairness, predictability, and equality among members. However, in practice, the system often reflects the power asymmetries between developed and developing nations. This paper critically examines the extent to which the WTO dispute mechanism is power-based rather than genuinely rule-based. Drawing on recent case law, trade disputes, and the challenges faced by weaker economies, the analysis demonstrates that while the formal structure appears neutral, outcomes frequently favour states with greater economic, political, and legal capacity. Key deficiencies, including limited access to resources for developing countries, the politicization of rulings, and enforcement asymmetries, highlight systemic inequalities. The paper concludes that unless reforms address these imbalances, the WTO will continue to reinforce existing power structures rather than serve as a truly impartial arbiter of trade disputes. Recommendations include strengthening support for developing states, enhancing compliance mechanisms, and ensuring that the principles of fairness and inclusivity underpin global trade governance.

title: Enhancing Fiscal Stability through Medium-Term Tax Strategies and Inflation-Adaptive Policies

detail.title: Enhancing Fiscal Stability through Medium-Term Tax Strategies and Inflation-Adaptive Policies
detail.abstract: Amid persistent macroeconomic volatility and inflationary pressures, international financial institutions have increasingly underscored the importance of fiscal consolidation as a cornerstone for sustainable public finance. Central to this objective is the adoption of mediumterm budgetary frameworks (MTBFs) featuring medium-term revenue strategies (MTRSs), which promote a coordinated, multi-year approach to tax reform that integrates policy design, administration, and legal structures. This paper examines the efficacy of medium-term tax plans, targeting the excisable goods market (e.g., alcohol, sugar-sweetened beverages, tobacco, fuel), by constructing a theoretical model comparing government revenue outcomes under a six-year rule-based plan with steady annual rate increases, against alternative biennial and triennial ad hoc tax adjustment scenarios. Furthermore, the analysis considers the revenue implications of indexation mechanisms (i.e., the automatic adjustment of tax rates to a select inflationary benchmark). Findings indicate that formal multi-year tax plans with scheduled annual increases markedly improve revenue stability and accumulation compared to ad hoc revisions. While indexation remains a useful mechanism for preserving the real value of revenues, it does not facilitate real revenue growth, underscoring the necessity for a dual strategy: utilizing indexation as a baseline safeguard to maintain the real value of revenues in inflationary settings, combined with formal multi-year tax plans. This dual policy allows governments to achieve real revenue growth, enhancing fiscal stability.

title: Energy Standard

detail.title: Energy Standard
detail.abstract: A currency backed by electricity, through its direct linkage to the watt-hour (Wh), issued at the moment of energy transmission and extinguished upon payment for electricity, offers not only internal economic and monetary stability but also a profound rethinking of economic thought. The integration of economics with the exact sciences, such as physics, fosters an expanded, interdisciplinary, and precise body of economic knowledge, enabling more accurate and efficient economic governance. The vulnerability of such a currency in foreign trade is addressed through the introduction of a dual-currency system, in which an external fiat currency functions as an intermediary layer, providing protection against manipulations in international exchange.

detail.abstract: This report summarizes the proceedings of the 2024 Patent Valuation and Damages Workshop: A U.S.–China Comparative Law Perspective, jointly organized by the Berkeley Asia IP & Competition Law Center (BAIC), Berkeley Center for Law and Technology (BCLT), KoGuan School of Law at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and the Institute of Intellectual Property and Competition Law. Held in Shanghai on May 28, 2024, the workshop convened leading judges, scholars, practitioners, in-house counsel, and economists from both countries to examine the evolving frameworks for patent damages and valuation. As the inaugural workshop on patent law and practice from a U.S.–China comparative perspective, pioneered by BAIC and BCLT, it explored compensatory damages (lost profits, reasonable royalties, price erosion, apportionment), punitive damages and their deterrence effects, the challenges of valuing and licensing standard-essential patents (SEPs), and the “important but limited” role of judicial rate setting in shaping technology markets. With attention to both theoretical underpinnings and practical case studies, the report highlights key similarities and divergences in practice, as well as the implications for global patent litigation and licensing. By capturing this pioneering comparative dialogue, the report provides valuable insight into the jurisprudential evolution of patent remedies and their broader policy context in the world’s two largest innovation economies.

title: A Comprehensive Real-Time Quantitative Framework for Option Pricing: Mathematical Foundations and Practical Implementation of the Heston Stochastic Volatility Model with Gauss-Legendre Quadrature

detail.title: A Comprehensive Real-Time Quantitative Framework for Option Pricing: Mathematical Foundations and Practical Implementation of the Heston Stochastic Volatility Model with Gauss-Legendre Quadrature
detail.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive quantitative framework for real-time option pricing that integrates the Heston stochastic volatility model with Gauss-Legendre quadrature methods and live market data acquisition. We develop a complete mathematical foundation starting from the fundamental principles of geometric Brownian motion and stochastic calculus, progressing through the derivation of the Black-Scholes equation and its limitations, and culminating in the rigorous mathematical development of the Heston model. The framework employs the numerically stable Little-Trap formulation of the Heston characteristic function and utilizes Gauss-Legendre quadrature for efficient Fourier inversion, achieving convergence to within 10-6 accuracy using 64 quadrature nodes. Our implementation includes comprehensive data acquisition capabilities through modern financial APIs, automated put-call parity validation, and extensive convergence analysis. Empirical testing using live market data from major equity indices (SPY, AAPL, TSLA, AMZN, GOOG) demonstrates that Heston prices can exceed Black-Scholes by several hundred percent for in-the-money options while maintaining positive values for deep out-of-the-money strikes where Black-Scholes approaches zero, effectively capturing the volatility skew and tail-risk premium characteristic of real option markets. The framework provides a robust foundation for quantitative finance applications, algorithmic trading strategies, and risk management systems.

title: The Snowden Leaks: An Analysis of Privacy, Security, and Democratic Accountability

detail.title: The Snowden Leaks: An Analysis of Privacy, Security, and Democratic Accountability
detail.abstract: This paper will cover the ethical, social, and political decisions and effects from 2013 revolving around Edward Snowden's leaks about U.S. government investigations. Covering a perspective from journalism, political communication, law, and international relations, I shall be discussing the support Edward Snowden received and the systems of government that supported him with the collected reforms, and what their assumptions are. The study provides a deep examination of the shift in the attitudes of the world-population towards the government and its functioning. This acknowledged change had a direct correlation to the modern inquiries about the functions and responsibilities of intelligence in open societies. By tracking the local and international impact of such revelations, the paper will discuss how these societal actions helped in sharp rethinking of policies and role transparency can have in democracies. The research states that when it comes to privacy rights and public debate, the political price for the action was fully worth it. The Department of Homeland Security defines a whistleblower as someone that performs an important service by reporting what they reasonably believe to be evidence of waste, fraud, abuse, or mismanagement (DHS). This is exactly what Edward Snowden did. In 2013 Edward Joseph Snowden went to Hong Kong and leaked thousands of top-secret documents about U.S. intelligence agencies' surveillance of American citizens to 3 journalists (Davies, 2019). By doing so Andrew Mitrovica, editor Al Jazeera, calls Snowden's leaks a courageous act because Snowden knew the blunt, life-altering risks he faced for sharing with the world the covert, often illegal, work done by spies at the National Security Agency (Mitrovica, 2022).

detail.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Nigeria’s Integrated Tax Administration System (ITAS) in Enhancing SME Financial Sustainability
detail.abstract: The increasing reliance on digital tax systems in emerging economies has positioned Nigeria's Integrated Tax Administration System (ITAS), particularly the TaxPro-Max platform, as a strategic tool for improving tax compliance and enhancing the sustainability of small and mediumsized enterprises (SMEs). This study evaluates the effectiveness of ITAS in reducing compliance costs, improving voluntary compliance, and fostering SME financial sustainability in Nigeria. A mixed-method research design was employed, combining quantitative data from 400 registered SMEs with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) and qualitative insights from in-depth interviews with Federal Inland Revenue Service (FIRS) officials. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, correlation, regression, and thematic analysis. Findings reveal that ITAS adoption significantly reduces compliance costs and administrative burdens, which positively influence voluntary compliance among SMEs. Furthermore, voluntary compliance mediates the relationship between ITAS adoption and SME financial sustainability, thereby strengthening SMEs' growth potential, profitability, and long-term survival. However, challenges such as poor internet infrastructure, limited digital literacy, and resistance to technological change hinder optimal system effectiveness. The study concludes that ITAS is a critical driver of sustainable tax compliance and SME resilience in Nigeria, provided its implementation challenges are addressed. It recommends targeted taxpayer sensitization, infrastructural support, and continuous system upgrades to enhance the efficiency of ITAS and the financial sustainability of SMEs.

detail.abstract: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, well-known as the "Iron Man of India," played a pivotal role in laying the foundations for inclusive governance and grassroots empowerment. His contributions are widely recognized in the context of national unification and administrative integration; however, his leadership legacy extends meaningfully to areas of public health, education, empowerment, and rural development. Patel recognized that India's socioeconomic transformation required strengthening villages, the backbone of the nation, through inclusive participation. His advocacy for women's education was not merely a social reform but a strategic necessity to enhance civic awareness and intergenerational progress. He emphasized accessible healthcare as a prerequisite for development, understanding that a healthy rural population is essential for sustained economic output. By integrating these dimensions, he sought to create self-reliant villages with informed citizens capable of participating fully in nation-building. This vision aligns closely with contemporary Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 3 (Good Health), SDG 4 (Quality Education), and SDG 5 (Gender Equality), illustrating Patel's foresight in adopting a holistic, people-centric model. Revisiting his integrated framework offers valuable insights for addressing present-day rural challenges, where disparities in gender, health, and education still hinder progress. The paper reflects how his principles influenced later policies and structures, women's empowerment through participation, and the evolution of modern-day health missions.

detail.abstract: This study supports recent government reforms in disaster management and emergency response by aiming to clarify institutional roles across public and private sectors. Using institutional, complexity, and network theories, it explores how institutional arrangements and interactions can enhance emergency response effectiveness. Employing an in-depth research design, the study integrates qualitative and quantitative methods, with data collected through questionnaires, focus groups, interviews, document analysis, and expert consultations. Findings reveal that while institutional frameworks are acknowledged as influential, their impact is often perceived as limited due to weak implementation, fragmented structures, and a lack of support for collaboration. Addressing these issues could strengthen their role in fostering coordinated disaster management strategies. The study recommends reinforcing institutional frameworks through improved coordination, policy role clarification, and support for collaborative efforts. Moreover, Information and Communication Technology (ICT) plays a crucial role in integrating strategies and enabling timely responses. Finally, integrated disaster risk management is highlighted as a key driver for enhancing emergency operations and strengthening collaboration among institutions responsible for disaster response.

detail.title: Environmental Hazards, Household Adaptation, and the Gender Gap in Rural Labor Supply
detail.abstract: This paper examines how environmental hazards affect the gender gap in rural labor supply through the lens of resource allocation within households. Exploiting a unique heating policy in China, we employ a regression discontinuity difference-in-differences (RD-DD) design and show that exposure to severe air pollution significantly widens the gender gap in rural labor supply at both the intensive and extensive margins. Interestingly, the effects vary with household composition: women living with teenage children are more vulnerable, whereas those co-residing with grandparents are less affected. This pattern highlights caregiving responsibilities as the key mechanism: children primarily create caregiving demand, while their grandparents, despite being dependents themselves, can provide substitute care within the household. We also find that women earning less than their husbands are more likely to reduce their labor supply when facing environmental hazards, aiming to preserve the household utility. Based on our estimated elasticity of substitution between parental and grandparental caregiving, the counterfactual analysis indicates that meeting the WHO air quality standard would narrow the gender labor supply gap by 22.17% and 6.56% in households with and without co-residing grandparents, respectively.

detail.abstract: Chronic diseases like diabetes and hypertension account for nearly 90% of the $4.3 trillion U.S. healthcare spending in 2021. Mobile health (mHealth) technologies can help with preventive care and disease management by facilitating remote monitoring, enhancing patient engagement, and enabling timely interventions, but adoption is limited due to misaligned incentives. This paper addresses the challenge of designing effective payer-provider contracts to incentivize mHealth adoption for chronic disease management. We propose a direct revelation contract to overcome adverse selection (hidden patient health information) and moral hazard (unobservable provider effort). Patient health transitions are modeled using a discrete-time Markov Decision Process. We analyze the value of patient health information, defined as the difference in outcomes between a first-best scenario with full real-time data access by both providers and payers and a traditional office-visit model with limited observability. We then measure how information asymmetry affects contract effectiveness. Analytical and numerical results show that under certain conditions--especially when payers set high enough provider compensation caps--direct revelation contracts can achieve first-best outcomes. mHealth yields greater value when intervention costs are low and patient risk is high, and its informational benefits persist even with limited intervention effectiveness. These findings highlight the role of contract design in unlocking mHealth's potential and reducing agency costs in chronic disease management.

title: The Square Root of Geometry Dirac's Leap as a Compass for Today's Science of Complexity
affiliations: University of Birmingham

detail.title: The Square Root of Geometry Dirac's Leap as a Compass for Today's Science of Complexity
detail.abstract:
Physics has always been a dialogue between geometry and algebra. For centuries they walked separate paths, geometry with its curves and diagrams, algebra with its symbols and rules. Descartes first sketched a bridge with analytic geometry, mapping curves into equations. Newton and Leibniz then made the decisive union with calculus. Curves became derivatives, areas became integrals, and motion became algebraic law. Geometry and algebra had ceased to be strangers.

By the late nineteenth century physics faced a crisis. Maxwell’s field equations had unified electricity and magnetism but seemed inconsistent with Newtonian mechanics. The Michelson–Morley experiment failed to detect the ether that was supposed to carry light. Lorentz transformations worked formally but had no physical grounding. Poincaré suggested that relativity might be a principle of nature, while Minkowski later reimagined space and time as one geometry. Einstein’s 1905 paper cut through: the laws of physics are the same for all observers, and the speed of light is constant. The outcome was quadratic harmony: energy and momentum balanced within the geometry of spacetime.

Yet quantum mechanics spoke differently. It asked for probability, for the linear beat of time. The quadratic could not host both. Dirac stepped into this tension. He did not discard symmetry but transposed it. He moved Lorentz invariance from geometry into algebra, from the visible square of spacetime to the hidden anticommutators of matrices. In this act he renewed the marriage of geometry and algebra at a higher octave. Spin, antimatter, and new mathematics followed. The Dirac equation was not only a law for electrons. It was the square root of geometry itself, a resonance of the unity first sounded in calculus, carried through Einstein’s relativity, and renewed in the quantum world.

title: The Fallacy of a Colour-Blind Fed in Hidden Fallacies in Corporate Law and Financial Regulation (2025)

detail.title: The Fallacy of a Colour-Blind Fed in Hidden Fallacies in Corporate Law and Financial Regulation (2025)
detail.abstract: [T]he Fed’ s very existence and evolving institutional design, purposes and policies result from trade-offs that are often political and advanced by a limited set of interest groups. Though some scholars have made a  persuasive case for the political nature of the Fed, the literature is glaringly silent on the racial implications (if any) of such Fed politics. This chapter demonstrates that the interest groups who shaped the Fed excluded black economic experts invested in optimal economic outcomes for black communities and, in fact, were often actively hostile toward such outcomes. Indeed, the critical tradeoffs that would set the stage for so-called settled monetary policy occurred when black economic experts sought a seat at the table to much-belated avail. The consequence is a central bank that has centred and labelled as settled monetary policy the drivers of economic conditions closely linked to majority white experiences. This chapter contemplates how alternative policy choices might have defined the Fed ’ s monetary policy if due consideration were given to black economic outcomes. In doing so, it illuminates the structural racism embedded in the Fed’ s monetary policy that often results in ignoring harm to black households. The chapter offers a solution that compels the Fed to publicly account for its racial impact.

detail.abstract: The Philippine Electrical Code (PEC) is a collection of rules and regulations that regulate the safe and correct construction, operation, and maintenance of electrical systems across the Philippines. Becuran National High School currently has problems regarding the population of students, hence the need for new buildings to be built. But there are some neglected buildings not currently used today due to erosion of ceilings and mainly the lack of electrical supply and faulty outlets in the classrooms. This study aims to assess and install an improved electrical system in a public secondary school in Sta. Rita, Pampanga. The initial assessment revealed multiple issues, including faulty wiring, nonfunctional lighting, burned-out outlets, and damaged ceiling fans all of which posed safety risks. Thus, a new electrical system was designed that adhered to the Philippine Electrical Code (PEC). The redesign included a modern lighting layout, upgraded power outlets, and removed branching. The installation phase successfully replaced defective components, installed lighting, and provided sufficient electrical outlets. The study succeeded in converting a faulty and malfunctioning electrical system into a code-compliant and modern system that meets the classroom's present and future requirements.

detail.abstract: This paper reports an anticipatory democracy study based on a mathematical, computational and simulation model of anticipatory systems and political culture in hybrid social-political environments. The model is based on the earlier theoretical developments of value mappings model (Voinea, 2021a, b), on the theory of incursive and hyperincursive anticipatory systems (Dubois, 1998a,b), and the anticipatory democracy theory (Bezold, 1978, 2010), and it is inspired by the philosophical, theoretical and methodological approaches on space and time in film theory, cinematography and storytelling (Panofsky, 1939; Deleuze, 1985/1989; Elsaesser, 2009). The model performance is enhanced by the application of mathematical and computational concept of incursion and hyperincursion to multiple space and time dimensions for achieving convergence on future state and computing the desirable futures. The Case Study describes the hybrid social-political environment modelled and simulated with the emotions, values and identity mappings extracted by visual, text and content analysis from the tv-streaming data in the early days of the Romanian anti-communist revolution in December 1989. The research methodology and simulation experiments build-up on early value mappings computational and simulation modelling (Voinea, 2021a, b; 2022a, b) and reveal that hybrid environments facilitate and reinforce the participation in political protests and political change phenomena by enhancing the public expression of emotions, the emergence of social values of cohesion and solidarity as well as the emergence of social and political polarization, and the dynamics of assuming multiple (political) identities as an expression of high-intensity participation in political protests. This research methodology has been employed in studying several political issues in experiments with hybrid environments in comparison with traditional physical social-political environments, like the role of TV-streaming in (a) facilitating and increasing emotional expression of support for democracy, (b) facilitating and increasing the polarization of society between old communist leadership and new democratic forces taking the lead in the Romanian social and political system. Experimental modelling and simulation results show that the social political system simulated as a (early) hybrid environment proved to facilitate and reinforce the emotional, value-based, and belief-based expressions of participants to political protests and to facilitate their assuming multiple identities. Hybrid environments influence political phenomena by facilitating and reinforcing political psychological expressions, behaviors, communication (political discourse). Emotion, value and multiple identity mappings provide for the anticipatory capabilities in hybrid environments defined as social-political systems. Applications of the research findings reported in this paper target research developments of modelling by value mappings in the areas with high emotional intensity and stress like healthcare systems, banking and financial markets, and art industries with high social and political impact like movie industry.

detail.abstract: This opinion piece explores Donald Trump’s tariff-centered trade strategy and its consequences for U.S. leadership. detail.title: Digital Currencies, Energy Security, and Environmental Challenges: A G7 Perspective
detail.abstract: This article presents a comprehensive analysis of the impact of cryptocurrencies on the economic and environmental security of the G7 countries, exploring both the potential risks and prospects. The study focuses on the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, and Japan, offering a detailed exploration of the increasing adoption of cryptocurrencies in these nations. Despite the benefits such as enhanced financial inclusion and cross-border transaction efficiency, cryptocurrencies pose significant challenges, including their use in illicit activities like money laundering and terrorism financing. The research critically examines the substantial energy consumption associated with certain cryptocurrency mining processes, particularly Proof-of-Work mechanisms, and their consequent environmental impacts, including carbon emissions, electronic waste, and air pollution. It investigates the corresponding energy policies and regulatory responses emerging within the G7 to address these concerns, alongside the development of more energy-efficient alternatives like Proof-of-Stake and the push for renewable energy in mining. The article critically examines these dual aspects, highlighting the measures implemented by regulators and policymakers to mitigate risks. It also delves into the evolving landscape of Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs) and their potential role in enhancing financial system efficiency and security, including considerations for their energy footprint. The study employs a robust methodological framework, combining statistical analysis of market trends, case studies, and policy analysis to provide a balanced view of the current state and future trajectory of cryptocurrencies in the G7 countries. By offering a nuanced understanding of both the opportunities and threats posed by digital currencies, including their energy and environmental dimensions, this article contributes to the ongoing discourse on their integration into global financial systems and their implications for sustainable economic security.

detail.abstract: Over the past few years, amid the pandemic and other crises in the world markets, food security in Africa has once again become a key issue in international relations. However, what is important for the food sovereignty of the continent is not only the uninterrupted supply of food but also the gradual localization of food production in Africa, which requires increased fertilizer consumption, making the transition from the concept of “food security” to “food sovereignty” relevant. In general, it can be argued that the problem of Africa’s food sovereignty is not related to land scarcity but primarily to Africa’s position in the global value chains in the world’s food markets, as well as its dependence on imports of semi-finished food products. The key role in maintaining import dependence is played by influential lobbying and financial groups, intermediaries linked to transnational corporations, traders, and a number of other international actors. Structural imbalances in economic development have so far prevented most African countries from producing fertilizers domestically, which has led to an increase in fertilizer imports. In recent years, Russian exporters have managed to significantly strengthen their presence in African food and agricultural markets, bringing their share of the African fertilizer market to 20%. This article deals with the main trends of the movement toward food sovereignty in Africa, primarily considering the role of fertilizers in this process. For the first time, an analysis of the strategies of major Russian fertilizer suppliers in Africa is provided.

detail.abstract:
The energy crisis in the European market continues. This process has resulted from a combination of factors: accumulated structural imbalances in global energy markets, the energy policies of individual European Union countries and the EU as a whole, the pandemic, and finally, the Special Military Operation that began in February 2022, which caused a reduction in Russian gas supplies to Europe. The EU was unable—if such a goal was even set—to painlessly replace Russian gas from other sources, among which Africa was expected to play a significant role. In the spring of 2022, European high-level delegations visited African countries almost every week, trying to secure increased gas supplies.

According to the author’s estimates, based on data from exporters, importers, and international organizations, African gas exports to the EU in 2022 amounted to 72 billion cubic meters—about 2 billion cubic meters less than in 2021. At the same time, most African exporters (or rather, the Western operators of LNG plants who control LNG marketing) redirected to the EU part of the volumes previously supplied to Asia. Also, in 2022, a new African country entered the global LNG market—Mozambique. In December, Spain received its first LNG shipment produced by Britain’s BP at the Coral Sul floating LNG plant on Mozambique’s offshore shelf.

Within this study, statistics from African exporters, European importers, and international organizations were analyzed. Based on the analysis of the domestic gas markets of African countries (Algeria, Angola, Egypt, Cameroon, Mozambique, Nigeria, Equatorial Guinea), the reasons for the overall decline in supplies are presented, along with forecasts regarding the dynamics of African gas exports to the European Union in the medium term.

detail.abstract: Corporate residence is a key element of tax systems, establishing a nexus that justifies taxation independently of income source or operations. Though globalisation and digitalisation have exposed flaws in residence criteria, the concept remains vital. Tax systems have evolved around it, creating a functional balance with other principles like source rules and anti-avoidance. Reform should aim to simplify domestic tests and align treaty rules with personal nexus, resolving dual residency through clear tie-breakers. While not perfect, residence supports legal certainty and fairness. Improving it is not just technical—it’s a moral duty to uphold dignity and the common good.

detail.title: Spanish Recessions 1850-2023: A Business Cycle Accounting Analysis

detail.abstract: This paper quantitatively analyzes six major recessions in the Spanish economy between 1850 and 2023 using an accounting framework that decomposes deviations from trend into structural components. The results identify two types of recessions: those driven by labour-aumenting efficiency-such as the fin de siècle Depression and the Great Depression-and those primarily shaped by the household labour wedge-namely, the Great Stagflation, European Recession, Great Recession, and the covid-19 crisis. Tax dynamics played a key role in the Great Stagflation, but not in the more recent crises. Openness and employment composition are informative about labour-aumenting efficiency trend, while institutional labour market features-such as temporary contracts and unemployment benefits-are closely linked to the household labour wedge. The analysis confirms the growing relevance of the household labour wedge in explaining macroeconomic fluctuations in Spain, even when accounting for a stochastic downward trend in hours worked.

title: Optimal Income Taxation under Wage Rigidity
affiliations: Indian School of Business

detail.title: Optimal Income Taxation under Wage Rigidity
detail.abstract: This paper revisits two central questions in optimal taxation: should capital income taxes be eliminated, and is uniform labor taxation optimal? I show that in economies with wage rigidity-common under strong labor protections or centralized bargainingcapital taxation becomes welfare-neutral. This neutrality allows the Ramsey problem to be decomposed into a master-subproblem structure where capital and labor taxes can be determined independently. The decomposition yields two striking results. First, optimal capital taxes are strictly positive and constant. Second, optimal labor taxes vary systematically over time, depending on the joint dynamics of productivity and wages: they should be front-loaded when wages are initially high or productivity is rising, and back-loaded otherwise. These results show how wage rigidity fundamentally reshapes optimal income tax policies, overturning classic benchmarks in public finance.

This paper proposes a simplified version of the Klein-Spady estimator, which is shown to be easy to implement, numerically relatively more stable, and with excellent small-sample and asymptotic properties.

title: Brittle Financial Health: The Male Crisis Hiding in Plain Sight

detail.title: Brittle Financial Health: The Male Crisis Hiding in Plain Sight
detail.abstract: This article introduces the concept of brittle financial health, a psychological and behavioural condition affecting men whose financial identity is tightly fused with traditional masculine roles of provision, control, and stoicism. Unlike conventional financial disorders such as anxiety or overspending, brittle financial health manifests as emotional containment, compulsive overfunctioning, and strategic withdrawal, often misinterpreted as resilience. Drawing on insights from financial therapy and behavioural finance, the article critiques the gender-neutral framing of financial distress and argues that current therapeutic models often misread male silence as resistance rather than a survival mechanism. It calls for a paradigm shift towards antifragile financial identity, advocating for identity diversification, behavioural elasticity, and temporal anchoring. The phenomenon is not merely clinical but systemic, with implications for financial planning, leadership, and mental health. By naming and decoding this hidden crisis, the article offers a framework for more adaptive and inclusive financial wellbeing strategies.

detail.abstract: Since the Soviet era, West Africa has been a key focus of Moscow’s foreign policy. During the Cold War, Ghana, Guinea, and Mali, under leaders like Kwame Nkrumah and Ahmed Sékou Touré, built strong ties with the USSR, which also supported Nigeria during its civil war. Post-USSR, Russia sustained engagement, with Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo’s 2001 Moscow visit marking its renewed African focus (Ramani 2023). West Africa’s proximity drives trade with Nigeria and Senegal exceeding US$1 billion, with Russian investments in oil, gas (Lukoil), and bauxite (RUSAL). Since 2020, Russia has deepened ties with Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso, emphasizing political, diplomatic, and military-technical cooperation, with economic ties emerging in 2024–2025. Russia promotes sovereign development in the Sahel, supporting economic independence and localized industries, alongside Turkey and the UAE. Stable macroeconomic indicators reflect this strategy’s success. Russia transfers public administration expertise to strengthen institutions and foster growth. Expanding ties with Algeria, Senegal, Ghana, and potentially ECOWAS, Russia supports humanitarian, economic, and security initiatives, prioritizing sustainable development and African integration to enhance sovereignty, reduce external dependency, and boost regional trade competitiveness.

title: From Bust to Boom: The Great Depression and Women's Fertility
affiliations: University of Montreal, University of Montreal - Center for Research and Development in Economics and University of Montreal

detail.title: From Bust to Boom: The Great Depression and Women's Fertility

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: The United States experienced dramatic swings in fertility over the course of the early- and mid-20th century. This paper presents a novel explanation for these changes, linking the Great Depression to the contemporaneous fertility bust in the early 1930s, the baby boom from the late-1930s through the 1950s, and the subsequent baby bust of the 1960s. Our empirical analysis is based on an event-study approach that links county-level measures of Depression severity to annual fertility rates over an extended 50-year time horizon. We find that the Great Depression can account for roughly half of the bust-boom-bust swings in fertility rates over this period. It can also account for large cross-cohort differences in lifecycle fertility pro les and completed childbearing. We present evidence for a mechanism that accounts for these patterns: the shock incentivized Depression-era women to delay childbearing and to increase lifetime labor force participation. This employment response, in turn, temporarily crowded-out economic opportunities for subsequent generations of women, contributing to their high fertility rates through the 1950s and early 1960s.

detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of receiving one additional week of paid vacation on labor market attachment among Norwegian workers aged 60+. Employing a triple-differences estimation strategy, we exploit age-based eligibility thresholds before and after a 2009 reform to identify causal effects. Our findings indicate that the extra leave has negligible effects on both employment, sickness absence and disability benefit receipt in the year workers first receive it. If anything, some workers use the additional vacation time to increase earnings from secondary employers. The results imply that policymakers should consider alternative measures to mandated leave to support an aging workforce.

detail.abstract: The paper discusses the limits of credit and capital subsidies to finance MSMEs in the presence of jobs-related externalities. Using a stylized model of the decision to lend to enterprises with different levels of risk, we show that instruments like credit guarantees are likely to exclude enterprises that have a higher social rate of return and a higher social value than some of those that get access to credit. We also show that pigouvian wage subsidies equal to the value of the jobs externality are unlikely to be an efficient policy instrument; they would need to be firm specific and do not change the distribution of financial risks.  We argue that impact investment funds focused on jobs (IIFJ)  can be a market mechanism to channel part of existing government subsidies and deal with market failures resulting from both asymmetric information and jobs externalities.  Using an extended version of the model that is calibrated to a representative country we show that -- if well designed -- IIFJ can generate significant welfare gains relative to traditional investment funds because of their impact on jobs.

title: Social Risk, Fairness Types, and Redistribution

detail.title: Social Risk, Fairness Types, and Redistribution

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Inequality often arises from strategic interactions among individuals. This is so because risky investments can not only be resolved by chance (natural risk), but also by others actions (social risk). We study how these different sources of inequality shape fairness judgments and the level of redistribution in a controlled experiment with a total of 2,152 participants. We find significantly less inequality acceptance, and thus much more redistribution, under social risk. In addition to the well-known types of Libertarians, Egalitarians and Choice Egalitarians, we identify a novel, hitherto unnoticed, fairness type  Insurers  who always compensate unlucky risk-takers and are especially prevalent when one is let down by others rather than simply unlucky by chance. This suggests that impartial spectators view betrayal as more deserving of support than bad luck. Our findings show that fairness ideals depend jointly on risk-taking and the way in which risk is resolved, either by nature or another human actor, thus highlighting the important role of strategic interaction for fairness types and redistribution.

title: Citizen Training and the Urban Waste Footprint
affiliations: London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Centre for Economic Performance (CEP),  and London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Centre for Economic Performance (CEP)

detail.title: Citizen Training and the Urban Waste Footprint

detail.abstract: Diverting waste away from and zero waste to landfills are key sustainability policy aims of local and national governments around the world, particularly in countries with large waste footprints from rapid consumption growth and urbanisation. Segregation at the source of waste generation can offer a low-cost solution to urban waste footprints, yet segregation rates are low in many places, especially in the cities of developing economies. This paper studies a staggered randomised intervention offering training and education to citizens about waste segregation. Citizens in the city of Patna in India were given training on waste segregation at source, recycling and its environmental benefits in a large experimental intervention undertaken in collaboration with the city administration. Segregation-at-source increased substantially among households that received the intervention, and additional boosts to segregation arose from spatial spillovers, as the programme delivered at least a double-digit benefit-cost ratio. Citizen training, when effectively designed and implemented, does deliver a low-cost solution for the cities of developing countries to both reduce their waste footprint and enhance local environmental sustainability.

title: Board Gender Diversity and Workforce Composition, Compensation, and Retention for U.S. Publicly Traded Firms

detail.abstract: We use administrative data from the U.S. Census to estimate the effect of female director representation on workplace gender diversity and womens earnings. Using a difference-in-differences estimator that correctly accounts for variation in treatment timing, we show that first-time female director appointments lead to subsequent increases in workplace gender diversity. We find that the effects are driven by the improved retention of female workers in the middle and upper quartiles of the firms overall earnings distribution. We find suggestive evidence that the effects are due to the newly appointed female directors influence on corporate policy, as we observe stronger effects when the director is placed on one of the boards three core committees.

detail.title: Explaining World Savings

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System Research Series

detail.abstract: Saving rates are significantly different across countries and remain different for long periods of time. This paper provides an explanation for this phenomenon. We formalize a model of a world economy comprised of open economies inhabited by heterogeneous agents endowed with recursive preferences. Our assumed preferences imply increasing marginal impatience of agents as their consumption rises relative to average consumption of a reference group. Using measured productivity as the sole exogenous driver, we show that the model can not only reproduce the sustained long run differences in average saving rates across countries, but also provides a good fit to the time series behavior of saving observed in the data.

affiliations: Frankfurt School of Finance & Management, NHH Norwegian School of Economics , , University of Cologne and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

detail.title: News Customization with AI

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: News outlets compete for engagement rather than reader satisfaction, leading to persistent mismatches between consumer demand and the supply of news. We test whether offering people the opportunity to customize the news can address this mismatch by unbundling presentation from coverage. In our AI-powered news app, users can customize article characteristics, such as the complexity of the writing or the extent of opinion, while holding the underlying news event constant. Using rich news consumption data from large-scale field experiments, we uncover substantial heterogeneity in news preferences. While a significant fraction of users demand politically aligned news, the vast majority of users display a high and persistent demand for less opinionated and more fact-driven news. Customization also leads to a better match between the news consumed and stated preferences, increasing news satisfaction.

title: Environmental Summits and Innovation

detail.title: Environmental Summits and Innovation

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of Conference of the Parties (COP) summits on innovation using an event study framework. Innovation is measured by patent grants, distinguishing between the total number of patents and the number of patents in environmental technologies, based on the World Intellectual Property Organization classification. We find that hosting a COP summit leads to a significant and lasting increase in the total number of patent grants, with an average rise of about 35 percent per year from the seventh to the thirteenth year after the summit, but has only a limited effect on the number of patent grants in environmental technologies. We further examine potential heterogeneity in the effects of COP summits by analyzing the impact of hosting a summit on patents in environmental technology compared to other technologies separately for each host country. The results suggest that while hosting a COP summit generally promotes environmental patenting, the effect is negative in some countries. We discuss possible reasons, including diminishing returns in green innovation and the influence of large industrial emitters. The findings are robust across alternative estimators, the inclusion of control variables, and different measures of patenting activity.

title: Makers and Takers: The Economics of the Kalshi Prediction Market
affiliations: University College Dublin, University College Dublin and University College Dublin (UCD)

detail.title: Makers and Takers: The Economics of the Kalshi Prediction Market

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Since 2021, Kalshi has operated as the only federally licensed prediction market in the United States. Using transaction-level data on over 300,000 contracts, we provide the first systematic evidence on its pricing. Kalshi’s contract prices are informative and improve in accuracy as markets approach closing, but they display a clear favorite–longshot bias: low-price contracts win far less often than required to break even, while high-price contracts win more often and yield small positive returns. We interpret these patterns with a simple framework that reflects Kalshi’s quote-driven microstructure. Makers—relatively well-informed traders who post offers—seek positive expected returns but may be slightly over-optimistic, while Takers accept these offers. The model predicts distinct patterns of favorite–longshot bias for Makers and Takers, and the data confirm these predictions.

title: Why are Manufacturing Plants Smaller in Developing Countries? Theory and Evidence from India

detail.title: Why are Manufacturing Plants Smaller in Developing Countries? Theory and Evidence from India

detail.abstract: Poorer countries (and poorer states within India) have a larger share of manufacturing employment in small plants. This paper presents empirical evidence and a theoretical model to show that this relationship is driven by greater demand for lower quality goods in poorer regions, which can be produced efficiently in small plants. First, using data for India, we show that richer households buy higher price goods and larger plants produce higher price products. Second, we develop a model that matches these facts. Finally, we find that our model explains about forty percent of the cross-state variation in the size distribution of manufacturing plants in India.

title: Cooperative membership: A Pathway to Climate Resilience for Nepalese Farmers
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Institute of Agricultural Economics and Information

detail.title: Cooperative membership: A Pathway to Climate Resilience for Nepalese Farmers
detail.abstract: Climate change threatens millions of Nepal's rural farmers due to a lack of institutional support and low adaptive capacity. Agricultural co-operatives have emerged as a promising solution to increase farmers' resilience. Despite growing interest in agricultural co-operatives, their role in supporting climate adaptation strategies remains underexplored in Nepal. This study examines the associations of producer and multipurpose co-operative membership on the number of climate adaptation strategies adopted using survey data from 400 households across three agro-ecological zones of Nepal. Propensity Score Matching (PSM) findings reveal that co-operative membership significantly increases the number of climate change adaptation practices adopted compared to non-members, regardless of the type of co-operative. The policies should focus on promoting and strengthening producer and multipurpose co-operatives that support farmers' access to resources, knowledge, and financial aid for effective climate adaptation. Encouraging co-operative membership via incentives and capacity-building programs can significantly boost farmers' adoption of climate adaptation practices.

detail.title: Analyzing citizens’ preferences for sufficiency policy in municipalities — An experimental approach
detail.abstract: Sufficiency policies address unsustainable consumption and production patterns by promoting ways of living and economies that prioritize “enough” over “more,” reducing resource use while safeguarding fundamental human needs. Public support is crucial for the effective implementation of sufficiency policies. Yet, empirical research on citizens’ preferences and the underlying mechanisms remains scarce — particularly in the form of quantitative studies and with respect to the municipal level. Thus, this study investigates public support for sufficiency policies in municipalities, focusing on governable factors that shape citizens’ preferences. Taking Switzerland as a case study, a nationwide representative online-survey (N=1052) was conducted, including a discrete choice experiment combined with a framing experiment. Our results suggest that citizens’ preferences for implementing sufficiency policies depend on the targeted policy sector, measure type, and procedural fairness. Firstly, respondents show the least support for housing sufficiency measures, rather opting for food or mobility sufficiency measures. Secondly, preferences regarding measure type depend on the designation and selection of specific policy measures, making general conclusions by type alone difficult. Thirdly, respondents place considerable emphasis on procedural fairness, favoring passive involvement in the implementation process by being kept informed. When strategically employing co-benefit framing to increase policy support, evidence on framing effects is mixed, but indicates that social co-benefits must be chosen carefully. Overall, we conclude that there is a modest but consistent majority in favor of implementing sufficiency policies at the municipal level.

title: Balancing Authority and Responsibility: Differential Impacts of Three Ecological compensation Policys on Local Water Governance Efficiency in China
affiliations: Lanzhou University, Lanzhou University and Fudan University

detail.title: Balancing Authority and Responsibility: Differential Impacts of Three Ecological compensation Policys on Local Water Governance Efficiency in China
detail.abstract: Watershed ecological compensation has become a key institutional innovation for addressing cross-jurisdictional water environment issues in global environmental governance systems. However, there remains a lack of systematic evaluation of how different watershed ecological compensation policies affect local government environmental behaviors and their differential effects. This paper integrates network governance theory with multi-level governance frameworks to construct a theoretical model for analyzing the policy effects of watershed ecological compensation, revealing how authority-responsibility structures, information transparency, and incentive modes shape local government environmental behaviors. Based on Chinese county-level panel data from 2008-2022, this study uses multi-period DID methods to comparatively analyze the incentive effects of three ecological compensation policies: vertical (central-local), unidirectional (local-local), and bidirectional (performance-based mutual compensation). The study finds that vertical and bidirectional ecological compensation policies have significant positive incentive effects on local governments’ water quality governance efforts, while the incentive effect of unidirectional compensation policies is not significant. These differential effects stem from variations in authority-responsibility structures, information transparency, and incentive modes under different compensation policies. The findings challenge the simplified assumption of centralization-decentralization dichotomy in traditional environmental governance and provide empirical support for “composite multi-level governance” that integrates polycentric governance principles with hierarchical control advantages.

title: Residential Relocation Decisions under Sea Level Rise and Incentives from Insurance: A Discrete Choice Experiment Study of France
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, VU University Amsterdam - Institute for Environmental Studies (IVM), VU University Amsterdam - Institute for Environmental Studies (IVM), affiliation not provided to SSRN, Institute for Environmental Studies (IVM)) and VU University Amsterdam - Institute for Environmental Studies (IVM)

detail.title: Residential Relocation Decisions under Sea Level Rise and Incentives from Insurance: A Discrete Choice Experiment Study of France
detail.abstract: This study examines household preferences for staying versus relocating under future coastal flood risk in metropolitan France, using a discrete choice experiment. By embedding Protection Motivation Theory (PMT) into a mixed logit framework, we account for both economic and cognitive drivers of residential decision making. Flood frequency, beach amenities, insurance premiums, and local economic outlook significantly influence staying preferences, while self-efficacy, homeownership, and social networks also play a key role. In contrast, perceived flood probability, general risk aversion, and income have no significant effect. In our counterfactual simulations, we find that insurance-based incentives are more effective than information provision alone in motivating relocation. Furthermore, high-income groups are more likely to remain in exposed zones across policy scenarios, although willingness-to-pay estimates suggest limited income-based sorting. However, the current uniform pricing structure of the French CatNat system may unintentionally reinforce the concentration of wealthier households in high-risk areas while shifting increasing future costs to the public. We also identify a parallel between risk-sharing insurance and the safe development paradox. As a remedy, we propose finer-scale risk-based pricing as a reform direction.

detail.title: Geopolitical Risk and Global Banking

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: International Finance Discussion Papers (Topic)

detail.abstract: How do banks respond to geopolitical risk, and is this response distinct from other macroeconomic risks? Using U.S. supervisory data and new geopolitical risk indices, we show that banks reduce cross-border lending to countries with elevated geopolitical risk but continue lending to those markets through foreign affiliatesâ  unlike their response to other macro risks. Furthermore, banks reduce domestic lending when geopolitical risk rises abroad, especially when they operate foreign affiliates. A simple banking model in which geopolitical shocks feature expropriation risk can explain these findings: Foreign funding through affiliates limits downside losses, making affiliate divestment less attractive and amplifying domestic spillovers.

title: The impact of forest land use on water charges: a geographically weighted regression analysis for Germany
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The impact of forest land use on water charges: a geographically weighted regression analysis for Germany
detail.abstract: Forests provide an important ecosystem service by supplying drinking water of high quality. Its economic value to society is reflected in reduced water treatment costs, among other things.  This study examines the influence of forest cover on drinking water charges across Germany, using geographically weighted regression (GWR) to identify regional variations. Unlike traditional spatial regression, GWR allows regression coefficients to vary across space, capturing differing effects of forest cover on water charges in different regions. The results reveal significant spatial heterogeneity in the relationship between land use and water supply costs, also highlighting the importance of water infrastructure, groundwater yields, and terrain slope. Forest cover reduces water charges in 59-73% of Germany, depending on model specification. In these regions, a 1% increase in forest cover leads to a 0.030% to 0.053% reduction in water charges, translating to annual savings of €3‑4 million. Areas without a significant forest effect are mostly located in the southwestern part of the country, where water is transported over long distances, and local land use therefore has minimal impact on water treatment costs. We conclude that analyses of large, water-rich regions like Germany should account for spatial heterogeneity in water supply and costs. This study lays the groundwork for spatially targeted economic incentive systems, such as payments for watershed services, to address regional disparities in the availability of clean drinking water and help overcome local water scarcity challenges.

title: OntoMotoOS as Philosophical Reinsurance: Between Abstraction and Concreteness

detail.title: OntoMotoOS as Philosophical Reinsurance: Between Abstraction and Concreteness
detail.abstract: This paper proposes OntoMotoOS as a novel “philosophical reinsurance” framework for AI safety, bridging speculative value theory and practical experimental platforms. We introduce OntoMotoOS as a hybrid meta-operating system of values, integrating classic ethical principles (e.g. Kantian universality, Millian harm) into computational filters . OntoMotoOS’s innovation lies in operationalizing abstract thought experiments via concrete simulation: it offers an “infinite interpretation” platform where philosophical concepts are engineered into algorithms and live experiments . By mapping individual identity (IAMF), social mesh (OntoOmnia), and legacy (Digiton Elysium) into a recursive system, OntoMotoOS creates a virtual-concrete laboratory for ethics. This framework contributes to AI safety by uniting theoretical constructs (human values as insurance) with an interactive environment (ontomotoos.ai), thus translating high-level thought experiments into testable scenarios and adaptive protocols .

title: Hybrid Human-AI Teams: Perspective on Evolving Leadership
affiliations: Steel Authority of India Limited, SAIL Refractory Unit

detail.title: Hybrid Human-AI Teams: Perspective on Evolving Leadership
detail.abstract: Leadership is entering a decisive transition as artificial intelligence shifts from being a backstage tool to becoming an active member of teams. This essay explores how the integration of AI alongside human professionals redefines the practice of leadership. Traditional skills such as empathy, communication, and vision remain vital, yet their expression changes in hybrid contexts. At the same time, new competencies emerge: AI literacy, orchestration of human-machine workflows, ethical oversight and resilience in the face of disruption. Drawing on organizational behavior and contemporary AI developments, the essay endeavors to reposition leaders as conductors of collaboration between humans and intelligent systems. The article highlights both risks and opportunities, offering insights for leaders who must preserve human dignity while harnessing AI's precision and scalability. The future of leadership will depend on curating this symbiosis to achieve sustainable performance and human-centered progress.

title: A Right to Encryption in the European Union's Charter of Fundamental Rights
affiliations: University of Copenhagen - Centre for Advanced Studies in Bioscience Innovation Law (CeBIL)

detail.title: A Right to Encryption in the European Union's Charter of Fundamental Rights

declarations.funderStatement: Work on this article was conducted at the University of Oslo under the aegis of the project "Security in Internet Governance and Networks: Analysing the Law" (SIGNAL), funded by the Norwegian Research Council and UNINETT Norid AS.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Columbia Journal of European Law, Volume 30, Issue 1, Pp. 52-76

detail.abstract:
This article posits the existence of a 'right to encryption' within the European Charter of Fundamental Rights ('Charter'), contending that it prohibits the legislative incorporation of encryption 'backdoors' in ubiquitous applications and devices as a matter of EU law. The argument draws from the Court of Justice of the European Union's jurisprudence on the essence of the right to respect for private life under Article 7 of the Charter. Other avenues for locating such a right, including the right to personal data protection and freedom of expression, are also explored. However, it is concluded that the right to encryption is most firmly anchored in the essence of Article 7.

Timely amidst the EU's growing interest in tackling the so-called ‘going dark’ problem caused by ubiquitous forms of encryption such as end-to-end encryption, the article contends that the right extends to Member States, thereby protecting against domestic laws that seek to undermine robust implementations of encryption. European lawmakers are urged to pursue options to mitigate the apparent ‘going dark’ phenomenon that are workable in practice and, ultimately, lawful.

title: From Dartmouth to A3: Toward a New Order of Intelligence and Systemic Governance

detail.title: From Dartmouth to A3: Toward a New Order of Intelligence and Systemic Governance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or institutional conflicts of interest related to the publication of this manuscript. The A3 framework presented herein is the result of independent research and intellectual development, grounded in interdisciplinary synthesis and civilizational inquiry. While the author is actively engaged in outreach to academic, governance, and philosophical communities to advance the A3 architecture, these efforts are undertaken in the spirit of pluralistic dialogue and do not constitute a commercial or proprietary interest.

detail.abstract: The Dartmouth Conference of 1956 inaugurated artificial intelligence (AI) as a research f ield by framing intelligence as a problem of symbolic problem-solving and computational logic. While historically generative, this paradigm assumed that intelligence could be formalized through representation, optimization, and prediction: an assumption increasingly inadequate in the 21st century. This paper contrasts the Dartmouth Proposal with the A3 Model (Aram–Aanavam–Adhikaram), a new order cybernetic framework that reconfigures intelligence as recursive ethical governance. Unlike the representational rationalism of Dartmouth, the A3 Model embeds ethics (Aram), distortion awareness (Aanavam), and agency fitness (Adhikaram) as endogenous drivers of system evolution. It is not an extension of symbolic AI or cybernetics but a reconstruction from first principles, drawing from Tamil Saiva Siddhanta metaphysics to address contemporary challenges in AI, complexity governance, and planetary resilience. The paper argues that where Dartmouth inaugurated AI as computation, A3 inaugurates intelligence as legitimacy fit for an age of recursive, autonomous, and ethically fraught systems.

title: The Impact of Fair AI's Recommendations on Human Decisions in a Hiring Process
affiliations: Case Western Reserve University, City University of New York (CUNY) - Paul H. Chook Department of Information Systems & Statistics and College of Business, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)

detail.title: The Impact of Fair AI's Recommendations on Human Decisions in a Hiring Process
detail.abstract: This study investigates the potential of bias-mitigated Artificial Intelligence (AI) in enhancing the fairness of hiring processes. While algorithmic decision support is prevalent in recruitment, algorithmic bias poses a significant challenge. Although methods to reduce such inevitable bias have been extensively studied, there remains a research gap as to how these algorithms can impact human decision-making. In this context, we explore how a fairlydesigned AI can minimize gender bias in a company's hiring process with a special emphasis on human and AI collaboration. By changing the protected attribute to the majority class, we first validate the fairness of the AI algorithm. Subsequently, we conduct an experiment in which participants are presented with randomly displayed fair advice from the algorithm and asked to make a hiring decision. Results indicate that such fair AI recommendations lead to less discriminatory decision-making, particularly among HR professionals. However, individuals lacking HR expertise or those who do not recognize gender bias in their workplace were less influenced by AI advice. Our study underscores the influence of AI usage familiarity and organizational culture on the adoption of fair AI systems. It suggests that targeted education and incentive programs are necessary to encourage wider acceptance of fair AI-driven decisions in recruitment, especially among those less accustomed to AI-assisted decision-making.

detail.abstract: This paper studies the drivers of the US real exchange rate (RER), with a particular focus on its comovement with net trade (NT) flows. We consider the entire spectrum of frequencies, as the low-frequency variation accounts for 62 and 64 percent of the unconditional variance of the RER and NT, respectively. We develop a generalization of the standard international business cycle model that successfully rationalizes the joint dynamics of the RER and NT while accounting for the major puzzles of the RER. We find that, while financial shocks are necessary to capture high frequency variation in the RER, trade shocks are essential for the lower frequency fluctuations.

title: Monetary Policy Transmission in Euroized Countries
affiliations: Cornell University, International Monetary Fund (IMF), ZEW – Leibniz Centre for European Economic Research, International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Monetary Policy Transmission in Euroized Countries

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper studies domestic monetary policy transmission in European countries with a significant share of lending and deposits in foreign currency, referred to as ‘euroized economies’. We find that the impact of domestic monetary policy shocks on both inflation and GDP diminishes with the degree of euroization across countries: the effects are twice as high in non-euroized countries compared to countries in our sample with the highest level of euroization. We further examine the exchange rate, credit and interest rate transmission channels, which are typically less effective in euroized economies. We show that domestic monetary policy has at best limited effects on the exchange rate. In addition, during the post-pandemic monetary tightening episodes, an increase in foreign-currency loans often softened the decline in overall credit growth, and rates of foreign-currency loans have followed the ECB policy rate rather than the domestic ones. By contrast, our analysis suggests that the pass-through to interest rates of domestic currency loans is similar across countries with different levels of euroization.
